title: Photosynthesis and breathing: how plants and other living beings share one breath

summary.text: Every dawn, fish in a still green pond swim up and gulp at the surface. The pond is full of plants that make oxygen, so why do the fish run short of it? Your child finds out with jars of cabbage-coloured water, a money plant and a window. A plant in light uses up the carbon dioxide you breathe out. The same plant in the dark adds carbon dioxide back, because every living cell breathes all day and all night. Then the idea goes out to ponds, to sugarcane and pineapples, to coal and oil, and to the carbon dioxide in the whole Earth's air, which falls and rises once a year.
summary.art: A green pond at first light with a few fish mouths at the surface, a cloud-covered sky, and a thin line of orange on the horizon.

intro.hook: A pond is full of green plants, and plants make oxygen. Yet at dawn the fish in the pond come up to the surface and gulp, as if they cannot breathe. Where did the oxygen go?
intro.text: You may already know that a leaf in the sun takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen. That is only half of the story. The same leaf also takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide, because every living cell needs energy from its food. Which half wins depends on the light. In this unit you catch the carbon dioxide in a jar, watch a leaf use it up in the light and add it back in the dark, and then work out why a pond runs short of oxygen just before sunrise.
intro.art: A jar of blue-purple water with a green sprig in it on a sunny windowsill, and an identical jar wrapped in foil next to it.

outcomes: I can explain that plants do both photosynthesis and respiration, and that the light decides which one wins overall.
I can run a fair test with a colour indicator, and use it to show that a plant takes in carbon dioxide in light and adds carbon dioxide in the dark.
I can explain why the oxygen in a pond is lowest just before dawn, and why fish gasp then.
I can compare photosynthesis and respiration: what goes in, what comes out, and where each happens inside a cell.
I can name three things that can hold photosynthesis back, and read a graph that shows it.
I can explain how sugarcane, maize and pineapple handle carbon dioxide and water in different ways from rice.
I can follow one carbon atom around the carbon cycle, and say why coal and oil are old sunlight.
I can say what scientists agree about, what they still argue about, and which scientists found out what.

terms.meaning: How green plants, algae and some bacteria build sugar from carbon dioxide and water, using the energy of light. Oxygen is left over. The word means 'putting together with light'.
terms.example: A tulsi leaf on a sunny windowsill is doing photosynthesis right now.
terms.art: A leaf in sunlight with arrows for light, water and carbon dioxide going in, and sugar and oxygen coming out.

terms.meaning: How a living cell gets energy out of sugar. The cell uses oxygen to break the sugar down, and gives out carbon dioxide and water. Plants, animals, fungi and bacteria all do it, day and night.
terms.example: Sprouting moong seeds respire, and get a tiny bit warm as they use up their stored food.
terms.art: A sugar molecule and an oxygen bubble going into a cell, with carbon dioxide and a spark of energy coming out.

terms.meaning: A tiny green part inside a leaf cell where photosynthesis happens. One leaf cell can have dozens of them.
terms.example: Under a toy microscope, a leaf cell of a water plant looks like a box full of green beads. Each bead is a chloroplast.
terms.art: A plant cell drawn as a room with many small green ovals inside.

terms.meaning: Tiny parts inside almost every cell of plants, animals and fungi where respiration happens. One of them is called a mitochondrion. They are the cell's power stations.
terms.example: A muscle cell in your leg is packed with mitochondria, and so is a cell in a growing root tip.
terms.art: A cell with a few green chloroplasts and many small orange bean-shaped mitochondria.

terms.meaning: The green colouring in leaves that catches the energy of sunlight. It soaks up mostly red and blue light and bounces green light back.
terms.example: Grass looks green because of the chlorophyll in the blades.
terms.art: A sunbeam falling on a leaf, red and blue arrows going in and a green arrow bouncing out to an eye.

terms.meaning: Tiny holes, mostly on the underside of a leaf, that open to let gases in and out. Carbon dioxide goes in, and oxygen and water vapour go out. One hole is called a stoma.
terms.example: A single leaf of a banana plant has millions of stomata, each far too small to see.
terms.art: A zoom into a leaf underside showing mouth-shaped holes with two bean-shaped cells around each.

terms.meaning: The two bean-shaped cells around each stoma. When they swell with water, the stoma opens. When they lose water, it closes.
terms.example: On a hot, dry afternoon the guard cells of many leaves go limp and the stomata close to save water.
terms.art: Two bean-shaped cells forming an open gap on one drawing and a closed gap on another.

terms.meaning: A gas with no colour or smell. Air has only a tiny amount, about 4 parts in every 10,000. You breathe it out, and leaves take it in to build sugar.
terms.example: The bubbles in a fizzy drink are carbon dioxide.
terms.art: A child breathing out dotted puffs towards a leaf, next to a bottle of fizzy drink with bubbles.

terms.meaning: Oxygen gas that is mixed into water so that fish and other water creatures can breathe it. Water holds far less oxygen than air does.
terms.example: Fish take dissolved oxygen out of the water through their gills.
terms.art: A fish with water flowing over its gills and tiny oxygen dots drifting in the water.

terms.meaning: A colouring that changes colour when something around it changes. Red cabbage juice is an indicator. It is blue-purple in water that is a little alkaline, and turns pink-purple when the water gets more acidic.
terms.example: Blow breath into blue-purple cabbage water, and it slowly turns pinker, because carbon dioxide makes water slightly acidic.
terms.art: Two glasses of cabbage water, one blue-purple and one pink-purple, with a straw bubbling in the pink one.

terms.meaning: The simple sugar that leaves make first. Its molecule has 6 carbon atoms, 12 hydrogen atoms and 6 oxygen atoms. Cells burn it in respiration to get energy.
terms.example: The sweet taste of a ripe banana is partly glucose, made in the banana plant's leaves.
terms.art: A ring-shaped glucose molecule drawn with six black carbon balls, twelve white hydrogen balls and six red oxygen balls.

terms.meaning: The one thing that is in the shortest supply and so sets how fast something can go. For photosynthesis it can be light, carbon dioxide, or warmth.
terms.example: On a dark, rainy afternoon, light is the limiting factor for a leaf, so adding more water makes no difference.
terms.art: A water barrel made of planks of different heights, with water spilling over the shortest plank.

terms.meaning: The light level at which a plant's photosynthesis exactly equals their respiration. At that light, no gas goes out or in overall. Below it, the plant is using up more than they make.
terms.example: A plant in a dim corner may sit just below the compensation point, so they slowly lose weight even though they are alive.
terms.art: A graph with two lines crossing at a dot labelled with a small sun, where making equals spending.

terms.meaning: A protein that speeds up one particular change inside a living body, without being used up. Every cell has thousands of different enzymes.
terms.example: An enzyme in your spit begins to break the starch in a piece of rice into sugar as you chew.
terms.art: A large curved protein shape with a small molecule fitting into a pocket and leaving as two pieces.

terms.meaning: A small molecule that picks up energy in one place in a cell and drops it off in another, like a rechargeable battery. The main one is called ATP.
terms.example: In a leaf, light charges up the energy carriers. Then the carriers give their energy to build sugar.
terms.art: A small battery shape being charged by a sunbeam on one side and plugged into a sugar-building machine on the other.

terms.meaning: The path that carbon atoms take round and round between air, living things, soil, the sea and rocks. Photosynthesis moves carbon out of the air. Respiration, rotting and burning move it back.
terms.example: The carbon in a mango was carbon dioxide in the air a few months earlier. It goes back to the air when you breathe out.
terms.art: A circle of arrows linking air, a tree, a child, soil with mushrooms, and the sea.

terms.meaning: Coal, oil and natural gas. They formed over millions of years from the bodies of plants and tiny sea creatures that were buried before they could rot.
terms.example: Petrol and diesel are made from oil. Burning them gives back carbon dioxide that plants and plankton took in long ago.
terms.art: A layer of ancient swamp ferns buried under rock, becoming a black seam of coal.

terms.meaning: A sudden, huge growth of tiny algae in water, which turns the water green. When the algae die, rotting uses up oxygen in the water.
terms.example: A village pond that turns thick green in hot weather has an algae bloom.
terms.art: A pond with thick green water, a few fish at the surface, and a dead patch of algae at the edge.

terms.meaning: A machine, or a simple tool, that mixes air into water so that more oxygen dissolves. Fish farms use them, especially at night.
terms.example: A fish farmer switches on a paddle that splashes the pond water, so that air mixes in.
terms.art: A paddle wheel on a pond churning white splashes, with air bubbles going down into the water.

terms.meaning: A plant that has a pump to gather carbon dioxide, so that photosynthesis goes fast even when the stomata are only a little open. Sugarcane, maize, sorghum and millets such as bajra and ragi are C4 plants.
terms.example: Sugarcane stays green and grows tall in the hot, bright months when many other plants slow down.
terms.art: A sugarcane leaf cut open, with a small ring of cells pumping carbon dioxide into a central bundle.

terms.meaning: A plant that opens the stomata at night to take in carbon dioxide and keeps them closed in the hot day. Pineapples, cactuses and Kalanchoe are CAM plants.
terms.example: A pineapple plant keeps a store of carbon dioxide made overnight, and uses it with sunlight the next day.
terms.art: A pineapple plant with open stomata under a moon at night and closed stomata under a bright sun in the day.

explanations.concept: Two jobs in one leaf: photosynthesis builds, respiration spends
explanations.definition: Photosynthesis uses light to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water, and gives out oxygen. Respiration breaks sugar down using oxygen to release energy, and gives out carbon dioxide and water. A plant does both.
explanations.description: Many people learn that plants take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen, and animals do the opposite. That is not quite right. A plant makes sugar only in their green cells, and only while light falls on them. But a plant needs energy all the time, to grow, to move water, to mend a torn leaf and to make seeds. So every cell in a plant, green or not, breaks down sugar by respiration, day and night. In bright light, a leaf makes much more sugar than they spend, so oxygen flows out and carbon dioxide flows in. In the dark, only respiration runs. Then the plant takes in a little oxygen and gives out a little carbon dioxide, just as you do. A plant grows when the sugar they make is more than the sugar they use. A plant kept in a dark cupboard for weeks keeps spending and never makes any, so they shrink and die.
examples: A money plant on a sunny windowsill gives out oxygen at noon and a little carbon dioxide at midnight.
A potato in a dark cupboard respires slowly, using up the starch they stored, and goes soft and wrinkled.
A root deep in the soil has no chlorophyll and no light, so they only respire. They live on sugar sent down from the leaves.
explanations.art: A leaf drawn in two halves, a sunny day half with a big arrow of oxygen out and a night half with a small arrow of carbon dioxide out.
explanations.context: Leaves make food in light. This card shows the other job that a leaf does all the time: spending that food.

explanations.concept: Where each job happens: chloroplasts build, mitochondria spend
explanations.definition: Photosynthesis happens inside chloroplasts. Respiration happens inside mitochondria. A green plant cell has both, and an animal cell has only mitochondria.
explanations.description: A cell is too small to see, but it is full of tiny parts. Chloroplasts are green because they hold chlorophyll. Inside them, light is caught and sugar is built. Mitochondria are smaller and have no colour. Inside them, sugar is broken down with oxygen, and the energy is stored in energy carriers that the cell can spend. A leaf cell has both. In the light, the chloroplasts make sugar, and some of that sugar goes into the cell's own mitochondria at once. The rest travels to the roots, the fruits and the growing tips. A human cell, or a mushroom's cell, has mitochondria but no chloroplasts. That is why we must eat. Our cells cannot make sugar from light, but they can spend sugar that others have made. A cell can have a hundred mitochondria, or thousands, depending on how much energy the cell uses.
examples: A cell in a pumping heart muscle is packed with mitochondria, because it spends energy all the time.
A potato tuber cell has no chloroplasts when it is underground, but it has mitochondria to spend the stored starch.
explanations.art: A plant cell and an animal cell side by side. The plant cell has green chloroplasts and orange mitochondria. The animal cell has only orange mitochondria.
explanations.context: Photosynthesis and respiration are two jobs. This card shows the two tiny places inside a cell where those jobs are done.

explanations.concept: The compensation point: the light where making equals spending
explanations.definition: The compensation point is the light level at which a plant's photosynthesis exactly equals their respiration. At that light, no oxygen and no carbon dioxide leaves or enters overall.
explanations.description: Picture a plant at night. There is no light, so they only spend sugar. Now slowly switch on a lamp. At first the light is very dim. The leaf starts making a little sugar, but still spends more than they make. As the light gets brighter, photosynthesis speeds up while respiration stays about the same. At one brightness, the two are exactly equal. That is the compensation point. The plant is just paying for their own living, with nothing left over to grow. Brighter than that, the plant has sugar to spare and grows. Dimmer, the plant is slowly using up their store. Plants that live in the shade of a forest floor, such as ferns, have a low compensation point, so they can live on very little light. Sun-loving plants such as sunflowers have a high one. This is why a sunflower grows weak in a dim room and a fern does not.
examples: A fern can live in the dim light of a shady corner, because they break even at a low light level.
A sunflower seedling on a gloomy windowsill grows long and weak. The light is below what they need to break even.
explanations.art: A line graph with light on the bottom and gas exchange on the side, a curve crossing a zero line at a dot labelled the compensation point.
explanations.context: Light decides whether a plant gains or loses sugar. This card names the light level where they exactly break even.

explanations.concept: Why a pond runs short of oxygen at dawn
explanations.definition: In a pond, plants and algae make oxygen only in daylight, but everything in the pond, including the plants, uses oxygen all the time. So the oxygen is highest in the afternoon and lowest just before sunrise.
explanations.description: Fish breathe the oxygen that is dissolved in water. Water holds much less oxygen than air does, and oxygen only slowly mixes in from the air above. A pond's main supply comes from the green plants and algae in it. In the day, they make more oxygen than the pond spends, so the oxygen level climbs and can be highest in the late afternoon. At night, the plants and algae stop making oxygen. But the fish, the plants themselves, the algae, the mud bacteria and the rotting leaves keep using it. So the level keeps falling through the night, and reaches its lowest point just before the sun comes up. If the night was warm and the day before was cloudy, the pond may have almost no oxygen left at dawn. Then the fish swim up to the top, where the water meets the air and holds a little more oxygen, and gulp. A fish farmer often runs an aerator in the second half of the night for this reason.
examples: A fish pond after three cloudy days has less oxygen at dawn than after three sunny days, because the algae made less oxygen in the dim light.
A fish farmer feeds the fish less on cloudy days. This protects the pond's oxygen, because uneaten food rots and uses oxygen too.
explanations.art: A line graph of oxygen in a pond over 24 hours, rising through the day to a peak in the afternoon and falling through the night to a low point at dawn, with a fish mouth at the surface.
explanations.context: Plants make oxygen, yet fish in a green pond gasp at dawn. This card explains why.

explanations.concept: Warm water holds less gas than cold water
explanations.definition: The warmer water is, the less gas it can hold. So warm water holds less dissolved oxygen than cold water.
explanations.description: Gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide dissolve in water, a little. Cold water holds more of them. As water warms, some of the gas comes out and forms bubbles. You may have seen this: a glass of cold water from the fridge, left on a table, grows tiny bubbles on the glass as it warms up. A fizzy drink goes flat faster when it is warm for the same reason. In a pond, this matters. In hot weather, the pond water holds less oxygen to start with. And the animals and rotting leaves in warm water use oxygen faster, because everything in a warm pond speeds up. So the hottest nights are the most dangerous ones for fish. The sea is the same. Cold seas hold more oxygen and are often rich with life, while a warm sea holds less.
examples: A bottle of cold fizzy drink stays fizzy longer than a warm one.
Tiny bubbles appear on the inside of a glass of cold water when it warms in a room.
explanations.art: Two glasses side by side, a cold one with few oxygen dots and a warm one with bubbles escaping from the glass walls.
explanations.context: A pond's oxygen depends on more than plants. This card explains why hot weather makes the problem worse.

explanations.concept: What holds photosynthesis back: limiting factors
explanations.definition: Photosynthesis can only go as fast as its slowest ingredient allows. The ingredient in shortest supply is the limiting factor. For a leaf it can be light, carbon dioxide or warmth.
explanations.description: Think of a kitchen with a cook, a stove and a pile of vegetables. If the stove is tiny, a second cook does not help. The stove is the limiting factor. A leaf is like that. On a dim morning, light is limiting. If you give the leaf more light, photosynthesis speeds up. But as the light gets stronger, a point comes when more light no longer helps, because the leaf cannot take in carbon dioxide fast enough. Now carbon dioxide has become the limiting factor. Warmth matters too. Photosynthesis uses enzymes, which are proteins that speed up changes inside a cell. Enzymes work faster when it is warm, up to a point. Very hot leaves slow down or get damaged. Greenhouse growers use this idea. They add light in winter, put extra carbon dioxide in the air, and keep the greenhouse warm, but not hot. They make sure that no single factor is the one that holds the plants back.
examples: A tomato plant in a closed greenhouse often grows faster when the grower adds carbon dioxide gas to the air.
In the shade on a cold morning, a leaf is limited by light and by warmth at the same time.
explanations.art: A water barrel with planks labelled light, carbon dioxide and warmth, and the shortest plank marked as the limit.
explanations.context: Plants do not make food at the same speed all day. This card explains what sets the speed.

explanations.concept: Inside the chloroplast: a light stage and a sugar-building stage
explanations.definition: Photosynthesis has two stages. In the light stage, chlorophyll catches light and uses it to split water, to give out oxygen and to charge up energy carriers. In the sugar-building stage, the charged carriers give their energy to join carbon dioxide into sugar.
explanations.description: Photosynthesis is not one step. It is a long chain of small steps, each done by its own enzyme. Scientists sort the steps into two groups. In the first group, which needs light, chlorophyll catches the light. The energy of the light splits water into hydrogen and oxygen. The oxygen floats away. The energy is stored in energy carriers, which are like small charged batteries. In the second group of steps, the carriers pass their energy to enzymes that take carbon dioxide from the air and join it into a chain of carbon atoms, which finishes as sugar. This second group does not use light directly, but it needs the charged carriers that only light can make. So it slows down soon after the light goes out. The steps were traced in the 1940s and 1950s by Melvin Calvin, Andrew Benson and James Bassham in California, who gave a plant radioactive carbon and followed it into sugar.
examples: A leaf moved into the dark keeps building sugar for a short time, using up the charged carriers that are left, and then stops.
The oxygen comes from the first stage, and the sugar from the second.
explanations.art: A chloroplast cut in half. Sunlight charges small batteries on one side. The batteries move to the other side and feed a machine that joins carbon dioxide into sugar.
explanations.context: Photosynthesis is often shown as one step, from carbon dioxide and water to sugar and oxygen. This card shows the two stages inside that step.

explanations.concept: Rubisco: the busy enzyme that sometimes grabs the wrong gas
explanations.definition: Rubisco is the enzyme that grabs carbon dioxide from the air and builds it into the first sugar. It is slow, and it sometimes grabs oxygen instead, which wastes energy.
explanations.description: Rubisco is the enzyme that takes the first step in building sugar from carbon dioxide. It is probably the most common protein on Earth, because a leaf needs a huge amount of it. Each rubisco works slowly, handling only a few carbon dioxide molecules every second. A leaf makes up for this by having a great deal of it. Rubisco has a weakness. It sometimes catches an oxygen molecule instead of carbon dioxide, because the two gases are similar in shape. When this happens, the leaf has to spend energy to clean up the mistake, and some carbon is lost as carbon dioxide. This is called photorespiration. It happens more when leaves are hot, because then the stomata close, carbon dioxide runs low inside the leaf, and oxygen builds up. Some plants, such as sugarcane and maize, have ways around this problem.
examples: Rubisco makes up a large part of the protein in green leaves. When you eat spinach, much of the protein you eat is rubisco.
On a very hot day, a rice leaf wastes more of their energy on photorespiration than on a cool day.
explanations.art: A big enzyme shape with a pocket. A carbon dioxide molecule fits in with a tick, and an oxygen molecule squeezes in beside it with a small cross.
explanations.context: Photosynthesis depends on one enzyme at the key step. This card shows that enzyme and its weak spot.

explanations.concept: Sugarcane and maize: a carbon dioxide pump (C4)
explanations.definition: C4 plants first grab carbon dioxide in outer leaf cells and pump it into inner cells, where rubisco works in a crowd of carbon dioxide. This lets them photosynthesise fast in heat and strong light, even with their stomata only a little open.
explanations.description: Most plants, including rice and wheat, hand carbon dioxide straight to rubisco. Sugarcane, maize, sorghum, bajra and ragi do something cleverer. Their leaves have a ring of outer cells and a ring of inner cells around each vein. The outer cells have a fast enzyme that grabs carbon dioxide and attaches it to a small molecule. The small molecule carries the carbon into the inner cells, which hold rubisco. There it releases the carbon dioxide, so that the inner cells have a lot of carbon dioxide and little oxygen. So rubisco rarely makes the oxygen mistake. The plant can keep their stomata nearly closed on a hot day, losing less water, and still make sugar quickly. This is why sugarcane grows so tall and sweet in India's heat. The pump costs some energy, so in cool, dim places a rice plant can do as well. The first clues were found in the 1960s by several scientists in different countries. Hal Hatch and Roger Slack in Australia worked out the steps. In India, Janaki Ammal, who was born in Thalassery in Kerala, worked on sugarcane breeding in Coimbatore in the 1930s.
examples: Ragi and bajra can grow in dry, hot regions where rice would struggle.
Sugarcane stores so much sugar in the stalk that we squeeze the stalk for juice.
explanations.art: A cross-section of a sugarcane leaf. Outer green cells grab carbon dioxide and pass it to inner cells around a vein. The sun beats down and the stomata are barely open.
explanations.context: Hot days make photosynthesis hard. This card shows one way that some plants beat the heat.

explanations.concept: Pineapples and cactuses: opening the stomata at night (CAM)
explanations.definition: CAM plants open their stomata at night, when it is cool, and take in carbon dioxide. They store it in acid form until morning, then use it with sunlight while their stomata stay shut.
explanations.description: A stoma lets carbon dioxide in, but it also lets water out. In a hot, dry place, a plant that keeps the stomata open all day loses a great deal of water. CAM plants solve this by working in two shifts. At night, the stomata open. It is cool, so little water escapes. The plant takes in carbon dioxide and locks it into an acid that is stored in big spaces inside the cells. If you taste a CAM leaf in the early morning, it can taste more sour than in the evening. In the day, the stomata close tight. The plant slowly releases the carbon dioxide from the acid, and the chloroplasts use it with sunlight to make sugar. CAM plants grow slowly, but they can live on very little water. Pineapples, cactuses, agaves, jade plants and Kalanchoe all work this way. A money plant on a windowsill is not one of them.
examples: A pineapple plant keeps their stomata open in the cool of the night.
A cactus can sit in a pot in a bright window for weeks without being watered.
explanations.art: A cactus under a moon with open stomata and carbon dioxide arrows going in, and the same cactus under a bright sun with closed stomata and sugar being made.
explanations.context: Some plants live where water is scarce. This card shows how they open their stomata at night instead of in the day.

explanations.concept: A carbon atom's trip: the carbon cycle
explanations.definition: Carbon atoms move round and round between the air, living things, soil, the sea and rocks. Photosynthesis takes carbon out of the air. Respiration, rotting and burning put it back.
explanations.description: Carbon dioxide is a very small part of the air, only about 4 parts in every 10,000. The air also holds nitrogen, about 78 parts in 100, and oxygen, about 21 parts in 100. Yet this thin supply of carbon dioxide is where almost every living body gets its carbon. Follow one carbon atom. It starts as carbon dioxide in the air above a paddy field. A rice leaf takes it in and builds it into sugar. The sugar becomes starch in a grain of rice. You eat the rice and your cells break the starch down by respiration, and the atom leaves in your breath as carbon dioxide. Back in the air, it may be caught by a tree or a phytoplankton cell in the sea. If a tree falls and fungi rot the wood, the atom returns to the air. If a tree is buried, the atom may stay locked in coal for millions of years. A carbon atom may make this trip many times. The atoms in your body are very old. Only the energy comes in fresh, as sunlight.
examples: The carbon in your breakfast idli was carbon dioxide in the air a few months ago.
A carbon atom in your breath can be taken in by a leaf in a few days, or by a tree that grows for a hundred years.
explanations.art: A circle of arrows: air, a rice plant, a child eating, a breath going out, a fallen log with mushrooms, a buried black layer of coal, and back to the air.
explanations.context: Photosynthesis and respiration pass carbon back and forth. This card follows one carbon atom all the way round.

explanations.concept: Coal and oil are old sunlight
explanations.definition: Coal, oil and natural gas formed from the bodies of plants and tiny sea creatures that lived millions of years ago, and were buried before they could rot. Their energy is sunlight that was caught by photosynthesis long ago.
explanations.description: About 300 million years ago, huge swampy forests of giant ferns and tree-like plants covered parts of the Earth. When these plants died, they fell into wet mud that had too little oxygen for the fungi and bacteria that rot wood. Layer upon layer built up and was squashed under rock for millions of years. Slowly the buried plants turned into coal. Oil and natural gas formed mostly from tiny living things in the sea, such as plankton, that sank to the sea floor and were buried in the same way. When we burn coal, petrol or diesel, the carbon atoms that photosynthesis took out of the air long ago return to the air as carbon dioxide, in a single lifetime. Plants take carbon dioxide out of the air slowly, and we have been putting back carbon dioxide from fossil fuels much faster than the plants and the sea can take it up. Coal is not made from dinosaurs. The coal forests grew many millions of years before the first dinosaurs.
examples: A lump of coal sometimes still shows the print of a fern leaf.
A bus running on diesel is driven by sunlight that fell on the Earth millions of years ago.
explanations.art: A timeline from a swamp forest with giant ferns, to the plants buried under rock layers, to a seam of black coal, to a power station chimney.
explanations.context: Burning coal and oil is part of the carbon cycle too. This card shows where they came from.

explanations.concept: When there is too much green: algae blooms and low-oxygen water
explanations.definition: An algae bloom is a sudden, huge growth of algae in water. When the bloom dies and rots, decomposers use up so much oxygen that fish and other water animals can suffocate.
explanations.description: Water that gets extra minerals can make algae grow wildly. The minerals can come from fertiliser washed off fields, from sewage, or from detergent that flows into a pond or lake. The water turns thick green, which looks healthy, and by day it can be full of oxygen. But a thick bloom blocks light from the plants below it, and at night the huge crowd of algae all use oxygen. Then the bloom dies, and bacteria and fungi rot the dead algae, using still more oxygen. The water can run so low that fish and crabs die in large numbers, sometimes in a single night. Some blooms also give out poisons. Scientists call large regions of water with too little oxygen 'dead zones'. Dead zones are found at the mouths of big rivers and in lakes around the world. Careful use of fertiliser and treating sewage before it flows into water helps to prevent them.
examples: Fish floating belly-up in a green pond after a hot, cloudy spell are often a sign of low oxygen.
Clear water with no fish and no plants is not always healthy, and green water is not always unhealthy. What matters is the balance between making oxygen and using it.
explanations.art: A pond turning from clear to green to dark, with fish gasping at the surface and a thick mat of algae dying at the edge.
explanations.context: Green water looks healthy, but it can be dangerous for fish. This card explains how too much of a good thing can use up the oxygen.

explanations.concept: The Earth breathes once a year
explanations.definition: The amount of carbon dioxide in the whole Earth's air rises and falls a little every year, because the land plants of the northern half of the world take in more carbon dioxide in their summer and give back more in their winter.
explanations.description: In 1958, an American scientist named Charles David Keeling began measuring the carbon dioxide in the air on a mountain in Hawaii, far from any city. He found something he did not expect. Every year, the amount of carbon dioxide went down in the northern spring and summer, and went up in autumn and winter. This small fall and rise repeats each year. The reason is that most of the Earth's land lies in the north. In the northern spring, forests and fields burst into leaf and their photosynthesis pulls carbon dioxide out of the air. In autumn the leaves fall and rot, and respiration by plants, microbes and animals puts it back. It is as if the whole planet breathes in and out once a year. Keeling's measurements also showed a second thing. Besides the yearly fall and rise, the amount of carbon dioxide has been climbing higher every year since 1958, because we burn fossil fuels.
examples: The yearly rise and fall can be seen in a graph of carbon dioxide over many years.
In India, many crops follow the monsoon. The land greens up each year after the rains, and the whole country's photosynthesis rises with it.
explanations.art: A globe with the northern half green in summer and brown in winter, next to a wiggly climbing line graph of carbon dioxide.
explanations.context: Photosynthesis is big enough to change the air of the whole Earth. This card shows how the carbon dioxide in the air falls and rises every year with the land plants of the north.

explanations.description: Rubisco sometimes grabs oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, and the leaf has to spend energy to repair the mistake. For a long time, many scientists have seen this as a flaw that evolution has not yet fixed. Now more scientists are asking whether it might do some good, too. This is an active question, and it matters, because if we could cut the waste, crops could grow faster.
examples: Engineers have tried to give plants a shortcut that avoids the wasteful cleanup. In some trials, the plants have grown more.
The cleanup process makes some building blocks that the plant needs, such as parts of proteins.

perspectives.explanation: Photorespiration is mostly a waste. It costs the plant energy and carbon. Rubisco evolved when the air had little oxygen, so the mistake did not matter then. Cutting down the waste could raise crop yields.
Photorespiration is not only a waste. It clears away a poisonous by-product, it makes useful building blocks, and it may protect the leaf from too much light. Removing it could harm the plant.

explanations.art: Two scientists looking at the same drawing of an enzyme. One has a thought bubble of a waste bin and the other has a thought bubble of a safety valve.
explanations.context: Scientists do not agree on whether photorespiration is a mistake. This card shows two views of it, and the evidence on each side.

explanations.concept: Can we make leaves better at their job?
explanations.description: A leaf stores only a small part of the energy of the light that falls on it. Scientists are testing ways to raise that. One group, led by Johannes Kromdijk and Stephen Long, changed tobacco plants so that their leaves recover faster when a cloud passes over after bright sun. In field trials, the plants were reported to grow about 15 percent more. Others are trying to build the sugarcane carbon dioxide pump into rice, or to add a shortcut that avoids the wasteful cleanup after rubisco grabs oxygen. These ideas are promising, but none is a quick fix. A plant is a very tangled system, and changing one step often changes ten others.
examples: A big project has been trying to give rice the sugarcane pump since 2008, and it has proved very difficult.
Some scientists are asking whether plants could be grown under coloured lights in towers, to use less land.
explanations.art: A rice plant with a small sugarcane-style pump drawn as a dotted addition, a scientist in a field with a clipboard, and a question mark above.
explanations.context: Hungry people depend on photosynthesis. This card shows scientists trying to improve it, and why it is hard.

agreed.text: Plants, algae and cyanobacteria do both photosynthesis and respiration. In light, photosynthesis is usually faster overall. In the dark, only respiration runs.
agreed.evidence: A plant in a sealed jar takes up carbon dioxide in light and releases it in the dark. This has been measured with gas sensors for over a century.

agreed.text: Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts, and respiration happens in mitochondria.
agreed.evidence: Under a microscope, chloroplasts are seen full of chlorophyll. Scientists have broken cells open and separated the two kinds of parts, and found that each does its own job.

agreed.text: Dissolved oxygen in a pond rises through the day and falls through the night, with its lowest point near dawn.
agreed.evidence: Fish farmers and scientists measure the oxygen in ponds with sensors. The same pattern appears in ponds all over the world.

agreed.text: The speed of photosynthesis is set by light, carbon dioxide and temperature, and the slowest of these is the limit.
agreed.evidence: Researchers put a leaf in a chamber and change one factor at a time. Each time, photosynthesis speeds up and then levels off, because another factor has become the limit.

agreed.text: Sugarcane, maize and other C4 plants, and pineapples, cactuses and other CAM plants, have extra steps that help them in hot or dry places.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have followed radioactive carbon into these plants and found different first products. The leaf structure of these plants also looks different under the microscope.

agreed.text: Coal, oil and natural gas come from the bodies of ancient plants and plankton.
agreed.evidence: Coal often contains the imprints of ferns and tree trunks. Oil contains chemicals that match those made by living things, and its carbon has the chemical signature of photosynthesis.

agreed.text: The amount of carbon dioxide in the air rises and falls a little each year as the northern land plants grow and die back, and it has been climbing steadily since 1958.
agreed.evidence: Charles David Keeling's measurements on a mountain in Hawaii, and many measurements since from stations around the world, show the same pattern.

agreed.text: Too many nutrients in water can cause algae blooms that lead to low oxygen and fish deaths.
agreed.evidence: Fish deaths and dead zones have been tracked to fertiliser and sewage flowing into rivers and lakes, and the zones shrink when the flow is reduced.

challenging.claim: Plants take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen, and animals do the opposite.
challenging.who: A rule taught in many schools and books for a long time
challenging.for: In daylight, a green plant takes in much more carbon dioxide than they give out, and gives out more oxygen than they take in.
challenging.against: A plant's cells breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide all the time. At night, the plant does only that. The plant is a net giver of oxygen only while the light is strong enough. Some animals, such as corals and sea slugs, even have photosynthesis going on inside them, some with the help of algae.
challenging.context: This card looks at the simple rule that plants and animals do opposite things with air.

challenging.claim: A pond with more plants always has more oxygen for the fish.
challenging.who: A common belief among people who keep fish
challenging.for: Plants make oxygen in the day, so a pond with more plants is full of oxygen in the afternoon.
challenging.against: At night the plants use oxygen too, and a thick growth can use more than the pond can supply. Dense plants and algae are often the reason the oxygen is lowest at dawn. The balance between making and using oxygen matters more than the number of plants.
challenging.context: This card asks whether adding more plants always helps a pond.

challenging.who: A simple answer from many school books
challenging.for: Leaves are flat, wide and full of chloroplasts, so most of the photosynthesis on a typical plant happens in them.
challenging.against: Green stems do photosynthesis, and so do green fruits and the green outer layer of many young trunks. A cactus has spines in place of leaves and does all of the photosynthesis in the stem. Algae and cyanobacteria have no leaves at all.
challenging.context: This card asks where in a plant photosynthesis happens.

challenging.claim: Yellow light works best for photosynthesis, because it is the brightest part of the rainbow to our eyes.
challenging.who: John William Draper, an English-American scientist, reported something like this in the 1840s.
challenging.for: To our eyes, yellow and green are the brightest colours, so it seemed natural that the plant would use them best.
challenging.against: In 1882, Theodor Engelmann showed that a green alga makes the most oxygen in red and in blue light, and the least in green. A plant's chlorophyll does not see colours the way our eyes do.
challenging.context: This card is about a mistaken idea that was corrected by watching tiny bacteria.

challenging.claim: Coal is made from dead dinosaurs.
challenging.who: A common idea in children's books and in conversation
challenging.for: Coal and dinosaurs both come from the distant past, and both are found buried in rock.
challenging.against: Most coal formed from swamp plants about 300 million years ago. The first dinosaurs came many millions of years later. Oil comes mostly from tiny sea plants and animals, not from big land animals.
challenging.context: This card asks where coal and oil really come from.

challenging.claim: Photorespiration is only a waste, and crops would be better without it.
challenging.who: Many plant scientists, but not all
challenging.for: It costs the plant energy and carbon, and plants with ways around it, such as sugarcane, grow very fast in heat.
challenging.against: The process also removes a harmful by-product and makes useful building blocks. Plants that cannot do it at all die in normal air.
challenging.context: This card is about a part of a leaf's work that scientists still argue about.

big_questions.q: A plant makes food and spends food at the same time. Is a plant a maker, a spender or both? And what about you?
big_questions.hint: Think about the money that comes in and the money that goes out in a home. Can a person be a maker and a spender?

big_questions.q: Fish gasp at dawn in a pond full of oxygen-makers. What does that tell us about the idea that more of a good thing is always better?
big_questions.hint: Think of how the oxygen in a pond rises by day and falls by night, and of the thick green bloom that blocks light and then rots.

big_questions.q: A carbon atom in your breath could have been in a tree, a mango, a dinosaur's world, or a fern in a swamp. Are the atoms in your body really yours?
big_questions.hint: How long have you held on to the atoms you ate last year? Where did they go?

big_questions.q: When we burn petrol, we are using sunlight from 300 million years ago. Who owns that sunlight?
big_questions.hint: Think about who will be here in 300 million years. Think about the plants that caught it.

big_questions.q: In 1882, Theodor Engelmann used tiny bacteria as his instrument to find where a green alga made the most oxygen, because the bacteria gather where there is oxygen. What other living things could we use as instruments instead of machines?
big_questions.hint: Think of a canary in a mine, or ants that find sugar. Is a living instrument easier to trust or harder?

big_questions.q: Sugarcane and pineapple found two different ways to beat the heat. Does a problem have only one right solution?
big_questions.hint: Sugarcane pumps carbon dioxide to where it is needed. Pineapple opens the stomata at night. Are both good?

big_questions.q: The Earth breathes in and out once a year, and we can see it from space. Is a planet something alive?
big_questions.hint: What would you need to see in a planet to say that it is alive? Do you see that in the carbon cycle?

big_questions.q: Photorespiration looks like a mistake, but it may do a useful job. How can we tell whether something in nature is a mistake or a good design?
big_questions.hint: Think about what we would have to know before we could decide. Who decides what a mistake is?

big_questions.q: Janaki Ammal, Kamala Sohonie and Penny Chisholm all did important science on plants and other photosynthesisers. Why do we often learn the names of only a few scientists?
big_questions.hint: Think about who gets into books, who gets prizes and who gets asked.

story.title: The Pond at Dawn
story.note: Anjana, her family, Beena Miss and the village are made up. The science in the story is real. In ponds, the oxygen in the water is usually lowest just before sunrise, and fish do come up to the surface and gulp then. Fish farmers do splash or churn the water, and feed less, to help. A real pond is harder to read than this one, and a farmer would also check the water with a meter.
text: Anjana lived in a village near Kumarakom in Kerala, where the backwaters spread out like green cloth. Behind her grandfather's house was a fish pond, a square of dark water with coconut palms around it. In the pond swam karimeen, the pearlspot fish that Kerala is proud of.

Every morning before school, Anjana carried a steel tumbler of rice bran to the pond and scattered it on the water. Her grandfather, Appooppan, stood beside her with his arms folded and counted the fish by their ripples. He was always right.
It was the monsoon, and for four days the sky had been grey. The rain came and went. The sun never really showed its face.

On the fifth morning, Anjana woke before dawn to the sound of Appooppan banging a pot. She ran outside in her nightdress. In the grey light, she saw something she had never seen before. All the karimeen were at the top of the pond. Their mouths opened and closed at the surface. Gulp, gulp, gulp.
'They cannot breathe,' said Appooppan. His voice shook. 'The pond has turned against us. Mathew's pond went like this last year. Every fish.'

Her uncle Gopan arrived on his bicycle, still wiping sleep from his eyes. 'It is the new feed,' he said. 'Or the water. We should drain the pond and fill it fresh. Or buy the white powder from the shop in Kottayam.' Appooppan nodded slowly at both ideas, which made Anjana nervous.
Anjana looked at the water. It was thick and green, much greener than last month. 'But Appooppan,' she said, 'a green pond is full of plants. Plants make oxygen. Beena Miss said so.'

Gopan laughed. 'Plants make oxygen, kutty, and the fish are choking. Which is it?' It was a fair question. Anjana did not know the answer. She stood very still, the way she did when a sum would not come.

Then she remembered another thing that Beena Miss had said. 'A plant makes oxygen only while the sun shines on it,' Miss had said. 'But a plant uses oxygen all the time, day and night, just like you. A plant sleeps and still breathes.' The whole class had giggled.

The sun finally came out a little after nine, a pale spot behind the cloud. By ten, the fish had sunk back down. By noon they were swimming in slow circles, as calm as ever. Appooppan went inside to eat, looking puzzled.

Anjana stayed at the pond. She watched the fish. She thought about how the trouble came only at dawn, and was gone by noon. The pond had not changed during the night. The fish had not changed. The only thing that changed was the light.

That evening, she found a blank page at the back of her notebook and drew a long line. On the left she wrote the night. On the right she wrote the day. She drew the green things in the pond making oxygen on the day side. On the night side she drew nothing, and then she drew arrows going the other way. Everything in the pond was using oxygen all night. The fish, the green things, the mud, even the old rice bran at the bottom.

'Appooppan,' she said at supper, 'I think I know. In the night, nobody in the pond is making oxygen, but everybody is using it. It keeps going down and down until the sun comes up. After four dull days, the green things made only a little in the daytime. So tonight there will be even less. It is worst just before sunrise. That is when the fish came up.'

Gopan scratched his head. 'Where did you get that?' 'From a jar at school,' said Anjana. 'And from the fish.' She took a breath. 'We can test it. Tonight we wake at four, and we stir the pond with the old boat paddle until the water foams. Stirring mixes in the air. If I am right, the fish will not come up. If I am wrong, tomorrow we buy your powder.'

It rained all evening. At four, Anjana's mother Sreedevi shook everyone awake, and carried a torch out to the pond. Appooppan, Gopan and Anjana took turns with the paddle. Frogs sang in the dark. Leela Chechi from next door came over in her raincoat to see what the noise was, and stayed to hold the lamp.

At five, Anjana counted the fish at the surface with the lamp. There were only three, and they were gulping slowly. Yesterday there had been all of them. 'No feed today,' she said. 'Food that nobody eats rots, and rotting uses oxygen too.' Nobody argued.

By nine, the sun had come out for real. Appooppan stood at the edge of the pond and counted the ripples. 'All here,' he said at last. He did not say anything about powder. Then he said, very quietly, 'Four grey days and I thought the pond was cursed. It was only short of light.'
Gopan handed Anjana the paddle. 'You have the night shift,' he said, 'if the clouds come back.'

A week later, the sun was strong at noon, and Anjana sat on a stone by the pond. Near the edge, silver beads of bubbles clung to the green threads in the water. Each one was a small breath, rising into the water. Above her, a coconut palm was using the air. Below her, the pond was too. She breathed out slowly. 'Share it,' she said to both.
story.epiphany: For the parent: plants and algae make oxygen only in light, but they use oxygen all the time, like every living thing. In a pond, nothing makes oxygen at night while everything uses it, so the oxygen is lowest just before sunrise. After cloudy days, the green things have made less to begin with, so the dawn is worse. Stirring the water mixes in air from above. Feeding less leaves less food to rot.
ask: In a pond full of green plants, why can the oxygen still run low just before sunrise?
Why would three cloudy days in a row make a pond more dangerous for fish than three sunny days?
How could you test, without a meter, whether the fish gulp because of a shortage of oxygen?
A fish farmer wakes at night to run a machine that stirs the water. Why at night, and not at noon?
If a plant uses oxygen all the time, how can a plant still be called a maker of oxygen?

A girl at a table at night drawing a long line in a notebook, with a day half full of green arrows and a night half full of arrows going the other way.
Four people with a torch and a wooden boat paddle churning a pond to white foam in the dark, in the rain.
A girl sitting on a stone beside a calm green pond at noon, with silver bubbles clinging to the green threads in the water.

printables.title: Tokens and pond to make at home
items: OXYGEN: cut 30 small squares of blue paper, or use 30 blue beads. This is the pond's oxygen supply.
PLANTS: cut 4 small green paper leaves. You start with 2.
FISH: cut 5 small paper fish. You start with 3.
POND: draw a big rectangle on a sheet of paper. The pond holds at most 12 oxygen. If it goes over 12, the extra is lost.

printables.title: Pond diary: write one line for each day
items: Day number and the action I chose
Oxygen at dawn after the night
What I would do differently next time

rules: Everyone plays on one team against the pond. The team starts with 8 oxygen, 2 plants and 3 fish in the pond.
The game lasts 6 days. Each day has four parts, in this order: choose an action, turn over a weather card, take away oxygen for the night, and check the pond at dawn.
Choose one action: ADD A PLANT (up to 4 plants), ADD A FISH (up to 5 fish), STIR AT NIGHT (add 2 oxygen during the night), or REST.

Turn over a weather card and follow it. Add oxygen to the pond for the day. Do all the adding and taking away for the day first, then drop any oxygen above 12. The pond can never hold more than 12 oxygen.
At night, take away 1 oxygen for every plant and 1 oxygen for every fish. Plants use oxygen at night because they respire all the time and there is no light.
If you chose STIR AT NIGHT, add the 2 oxygen before you take any away.
If the pond does not have enough oxygen for the night, take away all that is left. Then, at dawn, one fish dies for every oxygen that could not be taken away.
The weather cards are used once each. After 6 days, you win if at least 2 fish are alive. For a harder game, you must also have at least 4 oxygen left.
Playing alone, you make every choice yourself and keep the pond diary. Playing with others, you must agree on each action before you turn over the card.

flow.do: Draw the pond and cut out the tokens. Put in 8 oxygen, 2 plants and 3 fish. Shuffle the weather cards face down.
flow.say: This is our pond. It starts with 8 oxygen, 2 plants and 3 fish. We win if at least 2 fish are alive after 6 days.
flow.kid: Draw a pond. Put in 8 oxygen, 2 plants and 3 fish.

ask.q: What do you think will be the biggest danger to the fish?
good: Not enough sun.
The night.
Too many fish.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Write the guess at the top of the pond diary and look at it again at the end. With 2 to 4 players, share the jobs: one turns the weather card, one keeps the oxygen, one keeps plants and fish, one writes the diary. Swap jobs each day. Cards and tokens take about 10 minutes to cut out before the first game; beads or dried beans work for oxygen.
flow.context: This is the first step of Dawn Patrol. You set up the pond.

flow.do: Play days 1 and 2. Each day, choose an action, turn over a weather card, take away oxygen for the night and check the pond at dawn.
flow.say: Choose one action for today. Then turn over the weather card. Plants add oxygen in the day. At night, plants and fish take oxygen away.
flow.kid: Choose an action. Turn over a card. Plants add oxygen. At night, plants and fish use oxygen.

ask.q: Why do the plants take oxygen away at night?
good: Plants breathe too.
There is no light, so they cannot make oxygen.
Plants respire all the time.

check.q: In the game, plants add oxygen in the day and use oxygen at night. Why?
options: They make oxygen only in light, and use oxygen all the time
They are asleep at night and do nothing
They make oxygen from the moon
They only breathe out
check.why: Photosynthesis needs light, so it stops at night. Respiration does not need light, so it never stops. The option that says plants do nothing at night is a common wrong idea.

flow.parent: A new plant adds oxygen in the day but also uses oxygen at night. Let the child notice this before you say it.
flow.context: In this step you play the first two days and learn how plants and fish change the oxygen.

flow.do: Play days 3 and 4. Look at the oxygen count each dawn and write it in the diary.
flow.say: Look at the oxygen at dawn. Is it going up or down? What could you do about it before tonight?
flow.kid: Count the oxygen at dawn. Is it going up or down?

ask.q: On a cloudy day, does adding another plant help?
good: Not much, because the plant adds 1 and uses 1 at night.
It does not help, because the plant uses what it makes.
It makes no difference on a cloudy day.

flow.parent: On a cloudy day, a plant adds 1 oxygen and uses 1 at night, so they break even and do not help the fish. On a sunny day they add 2 and use 1.
flow.context: In this step you play days 3 and 4. A run of cloudy days can be dangerous.

flow.do: Play days 5 and 6. Count the fish left at the last dawn. Win if at least 2 fish are alive.
flow.say: This is the last stretch. Count the fish at the end of day 6. Did the pond make it?
flow.kid: Play days 5 and 6. Count the fish you have left.
flow.parent: If the pond lost fish, ask which day it went wrong and what the team could have done a day earlier.
flow.context: In this step you finish the game and count the fish.

flow.do: Read the pond diary together. Find the day with the most oxygen and the day with the least.
flow.say: Look at your diary. When was the oxygen highest? When was it lowest? What does that tell us about a real pond?
flow.kid: Look at your diary. When was the oxygen highest? When was it lowest?

ask.q: When was the oxygen lowest, and why?
good: At dawn, after the night.
Just before the sun came up, when nothing had made oxygen all night.
After a run of cloudy days.

flow.think: A real fish farmer cannot see the oxygen. How could the farmer tell that the pond was running low?
flow.context: This step looks back at the whole game and ties it to a real pond.
flow.parent: The game is meant to be hard. Adding fish first usually loses, and adding plants early and stirring at night when oxygen is low usually wins. It is fine to lose the first game and play again.

games.title: Who Is Doing What? Photosynthesis, respiration or both
games.players: alone, with a parent or with friends (1 to 4 players)
games.context: This is a card game. Each card names a living thing in a place at a time. You decide whether photosynthesis, respiration or both are happening, and explain why.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a pile in the middle of a table, with a sun token and a breath token in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Each player gets a sun token and a breath token.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud while the others each hold up one or both tokens in front of their chest.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone shows their tokens at the same time.

printables.title: 24 situation cards: a living thing and its place on the front, the answer and the reason on the back

items.f: A leaf of a money plant on a sunny windowsill at noon.
items.b: Both. Photosynthesis is fast, and respiration is running too. Overall, oxygen goes out.

items.f: A leaf of a money plant in a dark cupboard at midnight.
items.b: Respiration only. There is no light, so no photosynthesis.

items.f: A root deep in the soil of a pot.
items.b: Respiration only. A root has no chlorophyll and gets no light. They live on sugar sent down from the leaves.

items.f: You, running across the school ground.
items.b: Respiration only. Your cells are breaking down sugar with oxygen. Humans have no chloroplasts.

items.f: A fish in a pond at midnight.
items.b: Respiration only. The fish uses oxygen from the water through her gills.

items.f: Green algae in a pond at two in the afternoon, in strong sun.
items.b: Both. Photosynthesis is faster than respiration, so the water gains oxygen.

items.f: A mushroom growing on an old log.
items.b: Respiration only. Mushrooms are fungi. They have no chlorophyll and feed on the log.

items.f: Moong seeds sprouting in a dark box, pale yellow.
items.b: Respiration only. The sprouts have not made chlorophyll yet. They spend the food stored in the seed.

items.f: A green, raw mango on a branch in the sun.
items.b: Both. A young green fruit has chlorophyll and does a little photosynthesis, as well as respiration.

items.f: A cyanobacterium floating in sunny sea water.
items.b: Both. Cyanobacteria are tiny living things with chlorophyll. They do photosynthesis and respiration.

items.f: A baby sleeping at night.
items.b: Respiration only. All her cells are using oxygen to release energy.

items.f: The green stem of a cactus in bright sun.
items.b: Both. A cactus has no proper leaves, so the green stem does the photosynthesis.

items.f: A potato in a dark sack.
items.b: Respiration only, and very slow. The potato slowly spends their stored starch.

items.f: A bacterium in a heap of rotting leaves.
items.b: Respiration only. The bacterium uses oxygen to break the leaves down for energy.

items.f: A dry chana seed in a packet.
items.b: Almost nothing. A dry seed respires so slowly that they are nearly asleep. They wake up when they get water.

items.f: A leaf under a thick cloud at the end of a rainy afternoon, at the compensation point.
items.b: Both, and they exactly match. The leaf makes as much sugar as they spend, so there is no gas going in or out overall.

items.f: A leaf of red amaranth in the sun.
items.b: Both. A red leaf still has chlorophyll. Other colours hide the green.

items.f: A coral polyp in a sunny sea, with algae living inside her.
items.b: Both. The algae inside do photosynthesis and share sugar. The coral and the algae both respire.

items.f: A marigold petal in the sun.
items.b: Mostly respiration. A petal has little chlorophyll, so it makes very little sugar.

items.f: A chloroplast in a leaf cell in bright light.
items.b: Photosynthesis. The chloroplast is where light is caught and sugar is built.

items.f: A mitochondrion in one of your muscle cells.
items.b: Respiration. The mitochondrion is where sugar is broken down with oxygen to release energy.

items.f: A water plant and a fish in the same jar, with a black cloth over the jar.
items.b: Respiration only, for both. With no light, the plant makes no oxygen, and they compete with the fish for what is in the water.

items.f: A tree sapling in the deep shade of a forest at midday.
items.b: Both. Light is dim, so photosynthesis is slow. If the light is below the compensation point, the sapling is losing more than they make.

items.f: A banana plant at midnight.
items.b: Respiration only. The banana plant has no light, and uses the sugar they made during the day.

printables.title: Two tokens for each player
items: PHOTOSYNTHESIS: draw a bright sun on a card
RESPIRATION: draw a cloud of breath on a card

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card, reads the front aloud, and keeps the back hidden.
Every other player decides what is happening and picks the sun token, the breath token, both, or neither. They keep their tokens hidden against their chest so that nobody can copy.
Everyone shows their tokens at the same time. Then each player who wants a bonus point explains why in one sentence.
The reader reads the back. A player who showed the right tokens scores 1 point. A player who also gave a good reason scores 1 more.
Pass the reader job to the next player after each card. Play all 24 cards, or stop after 12 for a short game.
Playing alone, put the cards in a pile. Choose your tokens before you turn each card over, and score 1 point for each right answer. Try to beat your best score.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards. Give each player a sun token and a breath token.
flow.say: Each card tells us about a living thing in a place at a time. Is it photosynthesis, respiration, or both? Hold up your tokens.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Take a sun token and a breath token.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Is Doing What? You set up the cards and tokens.

flow.do: Play the first eight cards. After each card, read the back aloud and score the points.
flow.say: Read the card. Show your tokens together. Now read the back. Who was right? Who can say why?
flow.kid: Read a card. Hold up your tokens. Then check the back.

ask.q: Which things did only respiration, and what do they have in common?
good: They have no light or no chlorophyll.
They are roots, fungi, animals or things in the dark.
They all need energy.

check.q: A root in the soil has no chlorophyll. Which job does the root do?
options: Respiration only
Photosynthesis only
Both
Neither
check.why: Photosynthesis needs chlorophyll and light. A root has neither. But a root is alive and needs energy, so they respire. Anyone who picks neither has forgotten that roots are alive.

flow.context: In this step you play the first eight cards and learn how to score.

flow.do: Play the next eight cards. Keep score. Look for cards where both jobs happen.
flow.say: Keep going. Watch for cards where both jobs are happening. When is one bigger than the other?
flow.kid: Play eight more cards. Look for cards where both jobs happen.

ask.q: When both jobs happen, how can you tell which one is bigger?
good: It depends on how bright the light is.
In bright light, photosynthesis is bigger.
In dim light, respiration can be bigger.

flow.context: In this step you play more cards and notice that the light decides which job is bigger.

flow.do: Play the last cards and add up the scores. Talk about the card that surprised you most.
flow.say: Add up the scores. Which card surprised you most, and why?
flow.kid: Add up the scores. Which card surprised you most?
flow.think: Is there any living thing that never does respiration? What would that mean?
flow.context: In this step you finish the game and look back at the surprises.

items.p: What does a green plant do with the air during the night?
opts: Take in a little oxygen and give out a little carbon dioxide
Take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen
Nothing, because plants sleep at night
Take in only nitrogen
items.why: At night there is no light, so photosynthesis stops. But every cell of the plant still respires, so they take in some oxygen and give out some carbon dioxide. It is a common wrong idea that plants do nothing at night.

items.p: The job that needs light and builds sugar from carbon dioxide and water is called ____.
items.why: Photosynthesis means putting together with light. It happens in the green parts of plants, in algae and in cyanobacteria.

items.p: The roots of a plant do photosynthesis.
items.why: False. Roots under the ground get no light and have no chlorophyll. They respire, and live on sugar sent down from the leaves.

items.p: Blue-purple cabbage water turns pink when you blow into it through a straw. What does your breath add to the water?
opts: Carbon dioxide, which makes the water slightly sour
Oxygen, which makes the water pink
Heat, which changes the colour
Nitrogen, which bleaches the cabbage
items.why: Your breath has a lot of carbon dioxide. It dissolves in water and makes a weak acid, and cabbage water turns pinker with acid. Heat from the breath is far too small to change the colour.
items.context: In the Breath Colours test, you blow your breath into cabbage water and watch for a colour change.

items.p: Each of these belongs to photosynthesis or to respiration. Sort them.
items: Goes on in the day and the night
Breaks sugar down to release energy
items.a: see items
items.why: Photosynthesis needs light, happens in chloroplasts and gives out oxygen. Respiration happens in mitochondria, goes on all the time and releases energy from sugar. A strong answer keeps the two jobs apart.

items.p: Why do fish in a green pond often gasp at the surface just before sunrise?
opts: The oxygen in the water is at its lowest point then
The water is at its warmest then
The plants have made too much oxygen
The fish are hungry
items.why: All night, the fish, the plants and the mud use oxygen, and nothing makes any. So the oxygen is lowest just before the sun comes up. Too much oxygen would not make fish gasp.

items.p: Put these in order, starting from a sunny afternoon, to show what happens to the oxygen in a pond.
items: Plants and algae make lots of oxygen in strong light
The light fades and photosynthesis stops
Fish, plants and mud keep using oxygen all night
The oxygen falls to its lowest just before sunrise
The sun comes up and photosynthesis starts again
items.a: order shown
items.why: Oxygen rises while there is light. When the light goes, the making stops but the using goes on, so the oxygen falls until the sun returns.

items.p: Warm water holds more dissolved oxygen than cold water.
items.why: False. Warm water holds less dissolved gas than cold water. This is one reason hot nights are dangerous for pond fish.

items.p: Match each part of a plant to what it does.
pairs: Sugar is broken down with oxygen
Gases move in and out of the leaf
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Chloroplasts build sugar and mitochondria spend it. Stomata are the doors for gases, and the guard cells are the two cells that open and close each door.

items.p: A pot plant is kept in a dark cupboard for a whole month. What happens to the sugar the plant has stored?
opts: It slowly gets used up, because the plant respires and makes no new sugar
It grows bigger, because the plant is resting
It stays exactly the same
It turns into oxygen
items.why: In the dark, photosynthesis stops, but respiration goes on. The plant keeps spending sugar and makes none, so the store shrinks and the plant weakens.

items.p: Pineapples and cactuses open their stomata at night so that they lose less ____.
items.why: At night it is cooler, so less water escapes through the open stomata. These plants take in carbon dioxide at night and use it the next day, with their stomata closed.

items.p: A neighbour says, 'Plants make oxygen, so the more plants in a fish pond, the better.' Explain what could go wrong.
items.a: A strong answer says that plants make oxygen only in light. At night, plants use oxygen too, along with the fish and the mud. A very thick growth of plants or algae can use more oxygen at night than the pond has, so the fish may gasp at dawn. It also says that cloudy days make less oxygen, and that a balance matters more than a count.
items.why: The answer should show that plants both make and use oxygen, and that the night is the time of danger.

items.p: Use the words light and respiration to explain why a plant in a very dim corner might slowly lose weight even though they are alive.
items.a: A strong answer says that respiration goes on all the time and spends sugar. In very dim light, the plant makes less sugar by photosynthesis than they spend by respiration. So the plant is below the compensation point and slowly loses weight.
items.why: The answer should compare the sugar made with the sugar spent, and say that light decides which is bigger.

items.p: Draw a graph showing how the oxygen in a pond changes from one afternoon to the next morning. Mark the highest point with a sun and the lowest point with a moon.
items.a: A line that rises through the morning to a peak in the afternoon, then falls through the evening and night to its lowest point just before dawn. The sun is at the peak and the moon at the low point.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the lowest point near dawn, not at midnight, because the oxygen keeps falling all night.
items.art: An empty graph frame with time of day along the bottom and oxygen up the side.

items.p: Fish are gasping at dawn in a pond in Nagapattinam after three cloudy days. Three people say what to do.

views.says: Buy the chemical powder from the shop. It worked for my cousin.
Stir the water or run the aerator in the second half of the night, and feed the fish less.
Drain the pond and refill it with fresh water.

items.ask: What would you do first? Use what you know about oxygen in a pond. Then say one fair point for someone you disagree with.
items.a: Any choice can be strong if it uses the science. For example, stirring and feeding less is quick and cheap and fixes the missing oxygen. A strong answer says that the neighbour is right that fresh water has oxygen, but draining and refilling takes days and may harm the fish. It also says that the fish farmer's powder might help in some cases, but it does not add oxygen unless it is the right kind.
items.why: Stirring mixes air in at once and attacks the real problem, which is a lack of oxygen. The other ideas are slower or do not fix the oxygen. There is more than one reasonable view, so the reasons matter.

items.p: After three cloudy days, which one thing would most likely help a pond at 4 in the morning?
opts: Stirring the water to mix in air
Adding more fish
Adding extra food
Covering the pond with a cloth
items.why: Stirring mixes air from above into the water, which adds oxygen when nothing is making it. More fish and more food would use up more oxygen. A cloth would cut off even more air.

worksheets.title: Limits, Pumps and the Carbon Trip (stretch)

items.p: A leaf is at its compensation point. What is true about its gases overall?
opts: No oxygen or carbon dioxide leaves or enters overall
Oxygen leaves in large amounts
Only carbon dioxide enters
The leaf makes no sugar
items.why: At the compensation point, the sugar made equals the sugar spent. The oxygen from photosynthesis is used by respiration, and the carbon dioxide from respiration is used by photosynthesis, so nothing moves in or out overall. The leaf is still making sugar.

items.p: A leaf is in bright light, but there is very little carbon dioxide around them. Adding more light does not speed up photosynthesis. What is the limiting factor?
opts: Carbon dioxide
Light
Chlorophyll colour
The size of the pot
items.why: The limiting factor is the one in shortest supply. If more light does not help, light is no longer the shortest. Here carbon dioxide is.

items.p: A carbon atom in your breath may next be taken in by a ____.
items.why: Carbon dioxide in the air is taken in by leaves, and by algae and cyanobacteria in the sea. Then it is built into sugar, and the trip goes on.

items.p: Most coal was made from the bodies of dinosaurs.
items.why: False. Most coal formed from swamp plants about 300 million years ago, before the first dinosaurs. Oil formed mostly from tiny sea living things.

items.p: Sort these plants by when they mostly open their stomata.
items.a: see items
items.why: Pineapple, cactus and Kalanchoe are CAM plants, which open their stomata in the cool night to save water. Rice and wheat open theirs by day, and lose more water.

items.p: Match each plant to the way they cope with heat and water.
pairs: A pump that gathers carbon dioxide
Hands carbon dioxide straight to rubisco
Does photosynthesis in a green stem
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Sugarcane is a C4 plant with a carbon dioxide pump. Pineapple is a CAM plant. Rice has no pump and hands carbon dioxide straight to rubisco. A cactus has no proper leaves, so the green stem does the work.

items.p: Which stage of photosynthesis gives out the oxygen?
opts: The light stage, where water is split
The sugar-building stage, where carbon dioxide is joined
Respiration in the mitochondria
The closing of the stomata
items.why: The oxygen comes from the water that is split in the light stage. The sugar-building stage uses the energy carriers that the light stage charged up.

items.p: A graph of photosynthesis against light rises steeply and then goes flat. What does the flat part show?
opts: Something else, such as carbon dioxide or warmth, is now the limit
The plant has stopped being alive
Light has stopped being needed
The leaf has run out of water
items.why: When more light no longer makes any difference, light is no longer the shortest supply. Another factor has taken over as the limit.

items.p: Why does the amount of carbon dioxide in the whole Earth's air dip each northern summer?
opts: The land plants of the north are growing and taking in carbon dioxide
The northern oceans freeze
People burn less fuel in summer
The Sun gets brighter in summer
items.why: Most of the Earth's land lies in the north. When the leaves open in spring, photosynthesis pulls carbon dioxide out of the air. In autumn, the fallen leaves rot and give it back.

items.p: Put these in order along the trip of one carbon atom.
items: Taken in by a rice leaf and built into sugar
Stored as starch in a grain of rice
items.a: order shown
items.why: The atom goes from air to leaf to grain to child and back to the air. Photosynthesis takes it in and respiration gives it back.

items.p: Explain why a very green pond can still be dangerous for fish at night.
items.a: A strong answer says that a thick green bloom is a huge crowd of algae. By day they make a lot of oxygen. At night they all use oxygen and make none. If the bloom dies, it rots and uses even more. So the pond can run short of oxygen at dawn.
items.why: The answer should say that green means lots of living cells that use oxygen at night, and that dead algae use oxygen as they rot.

items.p: A fish farmer reads 1.5 milligrams of oxygen per litre at 5 in the morning. Many pond fish get stressed below about 3. What should the farmer do, and why?
items.a: A strong answer says to stir the water or run an aerator now, to mix in air, and to feed the fish less. The reading is well below 3, so the fish are in danger. Waiting for the sun to come up may be too late for some of them.
items.why: The answer should connect the number to a decision, and use the fact that the oxygen in a pond is lowest at dawn.

items.p: Draw the carbon cycle with at least five arrows. Include the air, a leaf, an animal, rotting and burning.
items.a: Arrows from the air to a leaf (photosynthesis), from the leaf to an animal (eating), from the animal to the air (breathing), from dead leaves and animals to the air (rotting by fungi and bacteria), and from fuel to the air (burning).
items.why: A strong drawing shows that carbon goes round, and that photosynthesis is the arrow that takes carbon out of the air.
items.art: An empty circle with room for pictures of the air, a leaf, an animal and a flame.

items.p: Photosynthesis happens only in leaves.
items.why: False. Green stems, green fruits and algae also do photosynthesis. A cactus does nearly all of theirs in the stem.

items.p: Three people discuss photorespiration, the mistake in which rubisco grabs oxygen instead of carbon dioxide.

views.says: It is a waste. If we could remove it, crops would grow faster and feed more people.
It is not only a waste. It clears a poison and makes useful building blocks. Plants without it die in normal air.
I do not care what it is called. I care whether the new seed gives more grain in my field.

items.ask: Which view do you find the most convincing? What evidence would change your mind? Say one fair point from someone you disagree with.
items.a: Any choice can be strong. A strong answer uses the idea that the process costs energy, but may also have uses. It names the evidence that would help, for example field trials that measure the grain from ordinary plants and from plants changed to avoid the waste, and tests of whether the changed plants are harmed. It gives the farmer credit that results in the field matter.
items.why: The scientists disagree about the facts, and the farmer cares about the result. Each view has a point, so the strongest answers use evidence and do not just pick a side.

items.p: Which sentence about sugarcane and rice is correct?
opts: Sugarcane has a carbon dioxide pump, so rubisco rarely grabs oxygen by mistake
