Rice has a carbon dioxide pump and sugarcane does not
Neither of them uses rubisco
Sugarcane opens stomata only at night
items.why: Sugarcane is a C4 plant. Its pump fills the inner cells with carbon dioxide, so rubisco rarely meets oxygen. Rice does not have the pump.

items.p: Look at the graph of oxygen in a pond on a cloudy day. About when is the oxygen lowest?
opts: At about 6 in the morning
At about 3 in the afternoon
At about noon
At about 9 at night
items.why: The line falls all night and reaches its lowest value, 1.5, at 6 in the morning. The peak, 4.5, is in the afternoon.
items.context: In the Pond's Day on Paper activity, you draw a graph of oxygen over a day and a night. This graph shows the cloudy day.

chart.title: Oxygen in a pond on a cloudy day (practice numbers)

items.p: Someone repeats the cabbage-water test with leaves in the light, but the jar is no pinker or bluer than the jar with no leaves. What is the most likely reason?
opts: Too few leaves, or too little light, for a change to show
Leaves cannot change the water at all
The cabbage water was too fresh
Jars must be kept in the dark
items.why: A leaf only takes up a little carbon dioxide each hour, so a small number of leaves or weak light may give a change too small to see. The fix is to use more leaves, give brighter light or wait longer.
items.context: In the Breath Colours test, you compare jars with and without leaves. This question is about a test that gave no clear change.

items.p: Air you breathe out has about 4 parts in 100 carbon dioxide. Ordinary air has about 4 parts in 10,000. Your breath has about ____ times as much.
items.why: 4 in 100 is the same as 400 in 10,000. 400 divided by 4 is 100. So your breath has about 100 times as much carbon dioxide as ordinary air.

items.p: When a leaf is moved into the dark, the light stage of photosynthesis carries on as before.
items.why: False. The light stage needs light, so it stops quickly. The sugar-building stage carries on for a short time, using the energy carriers that are left, then it slows down too.

items.p: Match each tool to what it tells you in this unit's tests.
pairs: A light meter or a phone app
How much oxygen is in the water
Whether the water has gained or lost carbon dioxide
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each tool measures one thing. Cabbage water is an indicator that changes colour with the acidity caused by dissolved carbon dioxide.

items.p: Which chain of events best explains how an algae bloom can kill fish?
opts: The bloom dies and rots, and bacteria use up the oxygen while they rot the dead algae
The algae eat the fish
The bloom makes the water too cold
The algae make too much oxygen
items.why: Rotting uses oxygen. A big bloom that dies at once feeds a big crowd of bacteria, which use up the oxygen the fish need.

items.p: A grower raises the light and the warmth in a greenhouse, but the plants grow no faster. What does this suggest?
opts: Carbon dioxide may be the limiting factor
Light is always the limit
Plants cannot grow faster than they do
The plants need less water
items.why: If raising two factors changes nothing, the limit is probably the factor that was not raised. A grower would test by adding carbon dioxide.

items.p: It is 4 in the morning at a pond. Sort each of these by what it would do to the oxygen in the water.
items: Painting the wall of the pond
items.a: see items
items.why: Stirring and breezes mix air in. Rotting food uses up oxygen, and on a hot night the warm water holds less. Fewer fish use less oxygen. Painting a wall changes nothing in the water.

items.p: Put these in order to show how too many minerals can lead to fish deaths.
items: Extra minerals wash into the pond
Algae grow in a thick bloom
The bloom dies and starts to rot
Bacteria use up the oxygen while they rot the dead algae
items.a: order shown
items.why: Each step causes the next. The key is that rotting uses oxygen, so the problem happens after the bloom, not only during it.

items.p: Design a test without a machine to find out if fish are gulping because of low oxygen. What would you compare, and what would you expect to see?
items.a: A strong answer compares the fish at different times, such as before dawn and at noon, or before and after stirring the water. It expects more gulping before dawn and less after the water is stirred or the sun is up. It keeps other things the same, such as feeding, and records the number of fish at the surface each time.
items.why: The answer should change one thing at a time and record what is seen. The test must be able to show the idea wrong as well as right.

items.p: Explain to a friend why it is not quite right to say that plants are givers of air and animals are takers of air.
items.a: A strong answer says that plants respire all the time, so they take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide like animals. In light, they make more oxygen than they use, so overall they give out oxygen. And some tiny animals and corals have algae that photosynthesise. Every living cell takes in and gives out, and light tips the balance.
items.why: The answer should replace giver and taker with the idea that every living cell does both, and light tips the balance.

items.p: A tree and a seam of coal both hold carbon that once came from the air. When was the carbon in each one last in the air?
items.a: A strong answer says that a tree holds carbon that was in the air during the tree's life, so within years or centuries. A seam of coal holds carbon taken from the air by swamp plants about 300 million years ago. Burning either returns the carbon to the air as carbon dioxide.
items.why: The answer should give two very different time spans and say that both go back to the air.

items.p: Sketch how you would expect the oxygen around a pot plant in a sealed bag to change from 6 in the morning to 6 the next morning. Mark where the plant is at the compensation point.
items.a: The oxygen starts to rise shortly after dawn, once the light is strong enough for the plant to reach the compensation point. It keeps rising through the day and peaks in the late afternoon or evening, when the light falls to the compensation point again. Then it falls through the rest of the evening and all night.
items.why: A strong sketch shows the plant at the compensation point twice: once in the morning, when the oxygen starts to rise, and once in the evening, when the light gets too dim and the oxygen peaks and starts to fall.
items.art: An empty graph frame with the time of day along the bottom and oxygen change up the side.

items.p: Three people argue about whether a greenhouse should add extra carbon dioxide.

views.says: Yes. When light and warmth are plentiful, more carbon dioxide gives us bigger tomatoes.
No. It costs money and burns gas. We should use sunshine and good soil instead.
Only if carbon dioxide is the limit. First measure which factor is holding the plants back.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use what you learned about limiting factors. Then say one fair point from someone you disagree with.
items.a: Any choice can be strong. A strong answer uses limiting factors: extra carbon dioxide only helps if it is the shortest supply. It gives the greenhouse grower credit that growth can rise, the organic farmer credit that the cost and burning of gas matter, or the plant scientist credit for testing first.
items.why: The plant scientist's view uses the idea of the limiting factor. The others each have a real concern. There is no single right answer, but wasted spending on a factor that is not the limit is easy to avoid.

items.p: Which situation matches the idea of the pond at dawn, where something is made and used at the same time?
opts: A water tank that fills from a small tap while a bigger tap at the bottom is open
A bottle with its cap on
A stone sitting on the ground
A lamp that is switched off
items.why: The pond's oxygen goes up when making beats using, and down when using beats making. A tank with water coming in and going out does the same. The level depends on which flow is bigger.

items.p: In sugarcane, the carbon dioxide pump means rubisco rarely grabs oxygen by mistake.
items.why: True. The pump fills the inner cells with carbon dioxide, so rubisco is surrounded by it and has little chance to grab oxygen.

items.p: A scientist finds that photorespiration protects a leaf in very strong light. What does this do to the argument about it?
opts: It supports the view that photorespiration is not only a waste, but it does not settle the question
It proves photorespiration is only a waste
It ends the argument for good
It shows that rubisco is not needed
items.why: One finding adds a reason in favour of one view. The debate is about the total of costs and benefits, which needs many tests in many plants and conditions.

experiments.title: Breath Colours: does a leaf use up the breath you blow into water?
experiments.question: Your breath makes cabbage water pinker. Will green leaves in the light turn it blue again? And what will the same leaves do in the dark?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After one day, which jar will be the bluest? Which will be the pinkest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All four jars hold the same amount of the same cabbage water. Jars A, B and C get exactly the same breath, one minute each. Jars B and C get the same number of the same kind of leaf. Only the light changes between B and C, and only the leaves change between A and B. Jar D has no breath and no leaves, so it shows the starting colour. Any difference in colour then comes from the leaves and the light. One child blows into all three jars, so every jar gets the same breath.
results_table: Colour after blowing, at the start
Colour after one day (ladder number, 1 blue to 5 pink)
Bluer or pinker than jar A?

materials.item: 4 clear jars with tight lids, each holding about 250 millilitres

6 big leaves of red cabbage, chopped small, and 5 cups (about 1.2 litres) of hot water (a grown-up pours it). If your tap or borewell water is hard, use filtered or boiled-and-cooled water, because hard water hides the colour change
a strainer or a clean thin cloth, and a bowl
a pinch of baking soda and a spoon
4 straws, one for each jar

two fist-sized bunches of one kind of water plant (hydrilla, elodea or hornwort from an aquarium shop or a pond, about Rs 30 to 50). House-plant leaves, such as money plant (12 per jar), also work but much more weakly
a lemon or a little vinegar, and 4 small clear cups, to make a colour ladder (see step 5)
aluminium foil, enough to wrap one jar all over
a white sheet of paper, a marker, a clock and a phone for photographs

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water. Blow out gently through the straw and never suck in, because the water is not for drinking. Stop and rest if you feel dizzy. Wash hands afterwards. Cabbage water stains clothes and fingers. Keep the jars where the sun is bright but the glass does not get hot to touch; hot water kills the plants. Wash the water plants first, and wash hands after touching pond plants.
experiments.record: Match each jar to the colour ladder and write its number. Photograph all four jars side by side on the white paper at the start and after one day. Colour in the table. Write your claim, your evidence and your reasoning.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you blow your breath into cabbage water, which changes colour. Then you find out what a leaf does to that breath in the light and in the dark.

setup.art: A bowl of chopped red cabbage with hot water poured on it, then a strainer pouring blue-purple liquid into a jar.
setup.caption: 1. Soak chopped cabbage in hot water, and strain it. The water turns blue-purple.

setup.art: A child blowing through a straw into a jar of blue-purple water that turns pink-purple, with a stopwatch showing one minute.
setup.caption: 2. Blow through a straw into jars A, B and C for one minute each. They turn pink-purple.

setup.art: Four jars in a row on a white sheet: A has only water, B has leaves in a sunny window, C has leaves and is wrapped in foil, D has no breath and stays blue.
setup.caption: 3. Put leaves in B and C. Wrap C in foil. Put all four jars at a sunny window.

setup.art: The four jars side by side on a white sheet the next day, D blue, A pink, B bluer than A, C pinker than A.
setup.caption: 4. Next day, compare the four colours on a white sheet.

flow.do: Show the jars, the leaves and the cabbage. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write both at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will blow our breath into cabbage water. Then we will put leaves in some jars. What do you think will happen? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We will blow into cabbage water. Then we add leaves. What will happen? Why?

ask.q: What do you think the leaves will do to the water in the light, and in the dark?
good: In the light they will use up the breath.
The dark leaves will not do anything.
Leaves give out air.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write it down so you can look at it again at the end.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Breath Colours test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up pours 5 cups (about 1.2 litres) of hot water over the chopped cabbage. Leave it 10 minutes. Strain it into a bowl and let it cool.
flow.say: Pour the hot water over the cabbage. Wait 10 minutes. The water will turn a deep purple. Strain it and let it cool.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to pour hot water on the cabbage. Wait 10 minutes. Strain it.
flow.parent: The water should look blue-purple. If it looks pink or red, stir in a tiny pinch of baking soda until it turns blue-purple. Use the same water for all four jars. Cold filtered water or boiled water gives the clearest colours. Hard tap water holds its colour and may show almost no change.

check.q: Why do we use the same cabbage water for all four jars?
options: So that every jar starts with the same colour
So that we use less cabbage
So that the water is warm
So that the leaves grow
check.why: If the jars started with different colours, we could not tell what changed them. The same water means a change comes from the breath, the leaves or the light.

flow.context: In this step, a grown-up helps you make the colour-changing water, called an indicator.

flow.do: Fill all four jars to the very top with the cooled water. Mark them A, B, C and D. Blow through a straw into A, B and C for one minute each.
flow.say: Fill every jar to the top. Blow gently through the straw for one full minute into A, B and C. Do not blow into D.
flow.kid: Fill four jars. Blow into A, B and C for one minute each.

ask.q: What colour is each jar now? Why do you think A, B and C changed and D did not?
good: A, B and C are pinker.
Our breath has something in it that changes the colour.
Breath has carbon dioxide, which makes the water slightly sour.

flow.parent: Time each minute with a clock. Photograph the four jars together on the white paper. Jar D stays blue-purple. A, B and C should look more pink-purple than D. If you cannot see a change, blow for two minutes in each jar, but give every jar the same time. Each blow should be gentle and slow, as if fogging a mirror. One child blows into all three jars, with a rest between, while a partner times each minute. With 2 to 4 children, share the jobs: blower, timer, jar-filler, photographer. With a bigger group, make two sets of jars so everyone has a part.

check.q: Why do we blow for exactly one minute into each of A, B and C?
options: So that each jar gets the same amount of breath
So that the jars get warm
So that the water bubbles longer
So that jar D turns pink as well
check.why: A fair test gives each jar the same amount of breath. If one jar got more breath, it could look pinker for that reason, and not because of the leaves.

flow.context: In this step, you put your breath into three of the jars and watch the colour change.

flow.do: Put one bunch of water plant into B and a bunch of the same size into C. Fill both jars to the top and close the lids tight. Wrap C all over with foil. Put all four jars at a bright window.
flow.say: Put one bunch of water plant in B and the same size bunch in C. Close the lids tightly. Wrap C in foil so no light gets in. Put all four jars in the light.
flow.kid: Add one bunch of water plant to B and the same to C. Wrap C in foil. Put all jars in the light.
flow.parent: Use fresh water plant of one kind. Weigh the two bunches, or judge them by eye, so that they are the same. Keep every jar full to the top with the lid on, because air above the water would change the result. With water plants the change often shows within 3 to 5 hours of sun, so peek in the afternoon. If the day is gloomy, leave them for two days. In very hot weather, move the jars to a bright but cooler spot.
flow.wait: Leave the jars for one day
flow.context: In this step, you add leaves and set up light and dark, then wait a day.

flow.do: Unwrap jar C. Put all four jars side by side on the white paper. Match each to the colour ladder. Photograph them. Colour in the table.
flow.say: Look at the four jars together. Which is the bluest? Which is the pinkest? What did you expect? What did you see?
flow.kid: Unwrap jar C. Look at all four jars. Which is the bluest? Which is the pinkest?

ask.q: What do you think the leaves in the light did to the breath? What did the leaves in the dark do?
good: The leaves in the light took the carbon dioxide out, so the water went bluer.
The leaves in the dark added carbon dioxide, so the water went pinker.
The light made the difference.

flow.parent: Make the colour ladder first, from spare cabbage water: put the same amount in 5 small cups and add 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 drops of lemon juice or vinegar, so they go from blue to pink. Number the cups 1 (blue) to 5 (pink); jar D is about 1. Expected with water plant: jar D stays blue. Jar A stays pink-purple. Jar B is bluer than A. Jar C is pinker than A. The changes can be small, so judge side by side on white paper. If all jars look the same, the plants may be too few or the light too weak, or your water is hard. Leave them one more day, or repeat with more plant. With house-plant leaves, expect little or no change; that is also a real result, so write it down.
flow.think: Jar A had no leaves and stayed pink. What does that tell you about the colour change in B?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the jars after a day and say what you saw.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what happened (the claim), what they saw (the evidence) and why it happened (the reasoning). Write one sentence for each.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think happened? What did you see to show it? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say what you think happened. Say what you saw. Say why.

ask.q: Why did the leaves in the dark make the water pinker, when leaves are supposed to be good for the air?
good: Leaves breathe too, and in the dark they only breathe.
In the dark there is no photosynthesis, but respiration keeps going.
They give out carbon dioxide at night, like us.

check.q: In this test, a jar with leaves in the dark turned pinker than a jar with no leaves. What does that show?
options: The leaves in the dark gave out carbon dioxide
The leaves in the dark took carbon dioxide in
The dark turned the water pink
Leaves do nothing in the dark
check.why: Pink means more carbon dioxide in the water. The leaves in the dark could not photosynthesise, but their cells kept respiring and gave out carbon dioxide. The choice that leaves do nothing in the dark is a common wrong idea.

flow.parent: A claim says what happened. The evidence is what you saw. The reasoning joins the two with the science. Accept the child's own words, and help them add the missing part.
flow.context: In this step, you say your claim, your evidence and your reasoning, as a scientist does.

schedule.what: Make the cabbage water. Blow into three jars. Add leaves. Wrap one jar in foil. Leave all four at the window.
Unwrap jar C. Compare the four colours side by side. Photograph them. Write the claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.title: Green Water: how much light does a pond need to turn green?
experiments.question: Tiny green algae can turn a jar of water green, if they get what they need. Does the green grow faster in the sun, in the shade or in the dark?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which jar will be the greenest after a week? Which will be the clearest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three jars hold the same amount of the same water from the same source, with the same tiny pinch of fertiliser. They are the same kind of jar and are covered in the same way. Only the amount of light changes: sunny window, shady corner and dark cupboard. So any difference in the greenness comes from the light. With 2 to 4 children, each child owns one jar and does the same jobs, or the children share the jobs of filler, scorer and recorder.

materials.item: 3 identical clear jars or glasses, each holding about 300 millilitres
about 900 millilitres of water that has stood open for a day, or rain water, or water from a pond or from under a pot plant
a spoonful of green water from a pond, a rain bucket or a fish tank, if you can find some (it makes the green start faster)
a tiny pinch of liquid plant fertiliser, or a few drops, the same in each jar. Without it, use one teaspoon of rice-washing water in each jar
3 squares of thin cloth or muslin, with rubber bands
a white card with a thick black cross drawn on it, a marker and a notebook

experiments.safety: Do not drink the water. A grown-up measures the fertiliser, which must be kept away from eyes and mouth. Wash your hands after touching it. Cover every jar with cloth, because uncovered standing water can breed mosquitoes. When the test is over, pour the water on the soil of a plant, away from the house. Wash hands after touching pond or tank water.
experiments.record: On days 1, 3, 5 and 8, hold each jar in front of the white card with the cross. Give it a see-through score from 0 to 3. Draw the three jars on day 8.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you grow a crowd of tiny floating plants in three jars with different amounts of light. You find out how light changes how green a pond gets.

setup.art: Three identical jars on a table filled with water, a spoon adding one drop of fertiliser to each, and cloth covers with rubber bands.
setup.caption: 1. Fill three jars with the same water. Add the same pinch of fertiliser. Cover each with cloth.

setup.art: Three jars: one on a sunny windowsill, one in a shady corner, one in a dark cupboard.
setup.caption: 2. Put one jar in the sun, one in the shade and one in the dark.

setup.art: A jar held in front of a white card with a thick black cross, the cross sharp in one jar, blurry in another, and gone in a third.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the black cross through each jar. Give a score: 3 is sharp, 0 is gone.

flow.do: Show the three jars and the water. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: Tiny green plants called algae live in pond water. We will give three jars different amounts of light. Which will turn greenest? Why?
flow.kid: We give three jars different amounts of light. Which jar turns greenest? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that jar will be the greenest?
good: It has the most light, and algae need light to grow.
The sun helps it.
The dark one will stay clear because nothing can grow.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Green Water test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Pour 300 millilitres of water into each jar. Add a spoonful of green water from a pond, a rain bucket or a fish tank to each, if you have it. Add the same tiny pinch of fertiliser to each.
flow.say: Pour the same amount of water in each jar. Add the same pinch of fertiliser to each. Make everything exactly the same.
flow.kid: Pour the same water in each jar. Add the same pinch of fertiliser.
flow.parent: Fertiliser feeds the algae. Use a very small amount, such as one drop or a pinch the size of a grain of rice. If you cannot find green water from a pond, a rain bucket or a fish tank, use water that has stood under a pot plant for a few days. The green may take longer to start. The best green water is from a bucket or pot saucer that has sat in sun for a week and looks slightly green.

check.q: Why do all three jars get the same water and the same pinch of fertiliser?
options: So that light is the only thing that changes
So that the water tastes the same
So that the jars weigh the same
So that the algae are not hungry
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one jar had more fertiliser, it might go green for that reason and not because of light.

flow.context: In this step, you fill the three jars and make everything the same except the light.

flow.do: Cover each jar with cloth and a rubber band. Put jar A at a sunny window, jar B in a shady corner and jar C in a dark cupboard.
flow.say: Cover each jar with cloth. This keeps mosquitoes out. Put one in the sun, one in the shade and one in the dark.
flow.kid: Cover each jar with cloth. Put one in the sun, one in the shade, one in the dark.
flow.parent: Choose places with the same temperature as far as you can. A shady corner could be behind a curtain, or under a table near the window. Mark each jar with a letter.
flow.context: In this step, you set the three jars in sun, shade and dark and wait for them to change.

flow.do: On day 3, bring each jar to the white card with the black cross. Give each a see-through score from 0 to 3. Write it in the table.
flow.say: Hold each jar in front of the card. Can you see the black cross sharply? Score 3 for sharp, 2 for blurry, 1 for faint and 0 for gone.
flow.kid: Hold each jar in front of the card. Can you see the black cross? Score it.

ask.q: Which jar is changing first? Is that what you expected?
good: The jar in the sun is going green first.
Nothing has changed yet.
I did not expect the shade one to change.

flow.parent: Use the same card, the same spot and the same lighting to judge every jar every time. Take a photograph too. If nothing has changed by day 3, wait. In warm sunny weather the green is usually clear in about 5 to 8 days; in cool or cloudy weather it can take two weeks, so keep scoring every 2 days if you need to.
flow.context: In this step, you check the three jars and score how green they are.

flow.do: On days 5 and 8, score the jars again. On day 8, draw all three jars side by side. Write your claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Score the jars again. Draw all three side by side. Which is the greenest? What does light seem to do?
flow.kid: Score the jars. Draw them side by side. Which one is greenest?

ask.q: Why does light make a pond turn green?
good: The tiny plants use light to make food, so they grow and multiply.
Light helps the algae grow and they make the water green.
More light, more green things.

check.q: The jar in the dark stayed clear. What does that tell you about algae?
options: They need light to grow and multiply
They are killed by cloth covers
They need darkness to grow
They are not alive
check.why: Algae make their own food by photosynthesis, and photosynthesis needs light. In the dark, they cannot make food, so they do not multiply. Algae are alive. They are tiny living plants.

flow.parent: If all three jars stayed clear after 8 days, the water may have had no algae to start, or the weather was cool. That is a real result. Add a spoon of green pond water and begin again, or carry on to day 12. If all three went green, check whether the shade jar got more light than you thought.
flow.think: In the story The Pond at Dawn, the pond had thick green water, and its fish still ran short of oxygen. What do you think thick green water does at night?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the three jars at the end and say what light does to a pond.

schedule.what: Fill and set up the three jars. Give each jar its first see-through score.
Score the three jars, draw them, and write the claim, the evidence and the reasoning.

experiments.title: Bubbles on the Glass: does cold or warm water hold more air?
experiments.question: Water holds some air inside it, which fish breathe. Does the water let the air go when it gets warm?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which glass will grow more tiny bubbles on its walls: the cold one or the warm one? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three glasses are filled from the same cold jug at the same time. They hold the same amount of water. Each stands in a bowl, and the only difference is the bowl water: icy, cool or hand-warm. Any difference in bubbles comes from the temperature.
results_table: Bubbles in a 2-centimetre patch after 10 minutes
Bubbles in a 2-centimetre patch after 30 minutes

materials.item: a jug of water chilled in the fridge for at least 4 hours
3 identical clear glasses
3 bowls that are deep enough to hold a glass
ice cubes, cool tap water and hand-warm water, about 40 degrees Celsius

a thermometer is best to check the warm water: a digital fever thermometer from a medical shop (about Rs 100 to 200) works. With no thermometer, the warm bowl should feel like comfortable bath water, so that you can keep a finger in for 10 seconds
a magnifying glass (stationery shop) or a phone camera zoom, a clock and a white sheet of paper

experiments.safety: A grown-up checks that the warm water is hand-warm, about 40 degrees Celsius, and never hot. Use glasses that are not chipped. Do not drink the water from the test. Keep the bowl water below the rim of each glass so none gets in, and stand the bowls on a flat place where they will not tip.
experiments.record: Note how many minutes pass before the first bubble shows. After 10 and 30 minutes, count the bubbles in a 2-centimetre patch of the glass wall (or score 0 to 5 if there are too many to count). Take a photograph of each. Write what you think the bubbles are.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you warm or chill the same water and watch for tiny bubbles. This shows what happens to the air that is dissolved in a pond when the weather turns hot.

setup.art: Three bowls in a row: one with ice cubes and water, one with cool tap water, one with hand-warm water, each with a glass standing in it.
setup.caption: 1. Stand three glasses of chilled water in bowls: icy, cool and hand-warm.

setup.art: A close-up of a glass wall with a few tiny silver bubbles clinging to it, held under a magnifying glass.
setup.caption: 2. Look at the walls of each glass. Tiny bubbles are air that came out of the water.

setup.art: Three glasses on a white sheet after 30 minutes, the warm one covered with bubbles, the cool one with a few, the icy one with almost none.
setup.caption: 3. After 30 minutes, give each glass a bubble score.

flow.do: Show the three glasses and the bowls. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess down.
flow.say: We will stand glasses of cold water in icy, cool and warm bowls. Which glass will get the most bubbles? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three glasses of cold water stand in an icy bowl, a cool bowl and a warm bowl. Which glass gets the most bubbles? Why?

ask.q: Where do you think the bubbles will come from?
good: From the air in the water.
From the glass.
The warm water boils a little.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Accept any reason.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bubbles on the Glass test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Prepare three bowls: icy, cool and hand-warm. A grown-up checks the warm water with a thermometer. Pour fridge-cold water into three glasses and stand one in each bowl.
flow.say: Make an icy bowl, a cool bowl and a hand-warm bowl. Check that the warm bowl is not hot. Pour cold water in the glasses and stand them in the bowls.
flow.kid: A grown-up helps with the warm bowl. Stand each glass in a bowl.
flow.parent: The warm bowl should feel like a pleasant bath, about 40 degrees Celsius. Pour all three glasses from the same jug at the same time. Do not shake the jug before pouring. With 2 to 4 children, give each child one glass and bowl to watch and score, and compare the scores at the end. In hot weather, tap water is already warm, so the cool bowl will be about room temperature, not cold.

check.q: Why do we pour all three glasses from the same jug of fridge-cold water?
options: So the water in every glass starts the same
So the glasses get heavy
So the bubbles are bigger
So the warm water cools down
check.why: If the glasses held different water, the bubbles could come from the water itself. The same cold jug means any difference comes from the bowl.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the three glasses in three bowls of different warmth.

flow.do: Look at the glasses after 10 minutes with the magnifying glass. Score the bubbles from 0 to 5. Wait and score again at 30 minutes.
flow.say: Look at the walls of each glass. Do you see tiny bubbles? Give each glass a score. Look again later and score again.
flow.kid: Look at each glass with the magnifier. Score the bubbles. Look again later.

ask.q: Which glass has the most bubbles? What are the bubbles made of?
good: The warm one. They are air that came out of the water.
The bubbles are gas, like oxygen.
Air that was dissolved in the water.

flow.parent: Expected: the glass in the warm bowl grows tiny bubbles first and the most, the cool bowl a few, and the icy bowl the fewest or none. The glass in the cool bowl also warms up to room temperature, so it may get bubbles later. Bubbles are small. Look closely, with a magnifier or phone zoom, against a white sheet. If you see no difference, the water may have been too warm to start; repeat with water straight from the fridge, and make the icy bowl really icy.
flow.context: In this step, you look for tiny bubbles and score them.

flow.do: Photograph the three glasses together. Write your claim, evidence and reasoning. Talk about what this means for a pond in hot weather.
flow.say: Which glass had the most air come out? What does that tell us about warm water? What could that mean for a fish pond in hot weather?
flow.kid: Which glass got the most bubbles? What does that tell us about warm water?

ask.q: If warm water holds less air, what might happen to the fish in a pond on a very hot night?
good: There is less oxygen for them.
They might gasp.
They use more oxygen because they are warm, and there is less to use.

check.q: In the test, the warm water grew more bubbles than the cold water. What does this show?
options: Warm water holds less dissolved air
Warm water has more air to start with
Cold water is full of air bubbles
The bubbles come from the glass
check.why: The glasses started with the same water. When some warmed up, the dissolved air came out as bubbles because warmer water cannot hold as much. A pond in hot weather has less dissolved oxygen for the same reason.

flow.think: On a hot night, a pond has less oxygen to start with, and the fish and plants use oxygen faster. What would you do if you looked after the pond?
flow.context: In this step, you say what the bubbles show and link it to a real pond.

activities.title: Stomata Prints: see the tiny doors in a leaf

materials.item: a thin leaf with a smooth underside, such as balsam, bean or tradescantia, still on the plant or freshly picked
clear nail polish and a small brush
clear sticky tape and a clean glass slide, or a flat piece of clear plastic
a magnifier: a clip-on phone microscope lens works best; otherwise a magnifying glass or your phone camera zoomed in close

activities.safety: A grown-up paints the nail polish, in a room with an open window, because the smell is strong. Keep it away from your face and from flames. Nail polish must never be swallowed or touched to the eyes. Nail polish catches fire easily, so keep any diya or match out of the room.

schedule.what: Paint a patch of nail polish on a leaf. Let it dry. Peel it off with tape. Look at the print.

activities.record: Draw what you see in the print. Count how many tiny mouth shapes fit in one small square of your view. Write which side of the leaf has more.
activities.context: In this activity, you make a copy of the skin of a leaf and look for stomata, the tiny holes that let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out.

setup.art: A grown-up painting a coin-sized patch of clear nail polish on the underside of a leaf.
setup.caption: 1. Paint a coin-sized patch of clear polish on the underside of a leaf.

setup.art: A strip of clear tape being pressed on a dry patch of polish and peeled away, then stuck on a glass slide.
setup.caption: 2. When the polish is dry, press tape on it, peel it off and stick it on a slide.

setup.art: A magnified view of a leaf print showing a pattern of cells with small lip-shaped pairs of guard cells around stomata.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the print under a magnifier. Find the stomata.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess how many holes a leaf has and where they are. Write the guess.
flow.say: A leaf must take in air. Where do you think the air goes in? How many holes do you think there are? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Where does air go into a leaf? How many holes? Guess.

ask.q: Do you think the holes are on the top of the leaf or the underside? Why?
good: The top, because the sun is on the top.
The underside, to keep the water in.
Both sides.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most leaves have more stomata on the underside.
flow.context: This is the first step of Stomata Prints. You guess before you look.

flow.do: A grown-up paints a patch of clear nail polish on the underside of the leaf. Wait 10 minutes for it to dry. Peel it off with clear tape.
flow.say: Paint a patch of polish on the underside of the leaf. Wait until it is dry. Press the tape on it and peel it off.
flow.kid: A grown-up paints the leaf. Wait until it is dry. Peel it off with tape.
flow.parent: Open a window for the smell. Make the patch about the size of a coin. If the polish lifts off in a clean thin sheet, it has worked. If it tears, make a thicker coat. Repeat on the top of the leaf in a different spot. With 2 to 4 children, each child picks a different leaf and a grown-up paints one patch for each. Clear nail polish costs about Rs 30 at a general store.

check.q: The polish print shows the shape of the leaf's skin. What does the polish do?
options: It sets into the shape of the skin, like a mould
It paints the leaf green
It kills the stomata
It makes the leaf grow
check.why: The liquid polish fills the tiny bumps and dips of the skin. When it dries and is peeled off, it keeps the shape, like a mould. It does not change the leaf.

flow.context: In this step, you make a print of the leaf's skin.

flow.do: Stick the tape with the print on a slide. Look at it under the magnifier. Find the tiny lip-shaped pairs of cells. Draw what you see.
flow.say: Look closely. Find the small pairs of curved cells with a gap between them. Each gap is a stoma. Can you count them?
flow.kid: Look through the magnifier. Find the tiny mouths. Draw what you see.

ask.q: Why might a leaf need so many tiny holes, and not a few big ones?
good: So that air can reach every part of the leaf.
Small holes can close easily to save water.
Many small holes let in more air without letting out too much water.

flow.parent: A phone clip-on lens that magnifies about 60 times works best (optional, about Rs 250 to 500). A plain magnifying glass or phone zoom shows the print only as a faint pattern of cell outlines, and the stomata may not be clear. That is fine: record what you can see, then count the cell outlines instead of stomata, or look at the print under a school or friend's microscope.
flow.think: A leaf can close the stomata. What would be the cost of closing them on a very hot day?
flow.context: In this step, you look for stomata in your print and draw them.

activities.title: Sun Leaf and Shade Leaf: same plant, two kinds of leaf

materials.item: a plant with some leaves in bright light and some in shade, such as a big potted plant, a tree or a bush, with permission to pick two leaves
squared paper, a pencil and a ruler
a magnifying glass
green crayons or colour pencils in 3 shades

schedule.what: Pick a sun leaf and a shade leaf. Compare their colour, size, thickness and feel.

activities.safety: Pick leaves only with permission, from a plant you know. Avoid plants with milky sap or thorns, and wash your hands afterwards.
activities.record: Make a table for the two leaves: the crayon colour that matches, the area in squares, the thickness by feel, and one other difference you notice.
activities.context: In this activity, you compare a leaf that grew in bright sun with a leaf that grew in shade on the same plant. You find out how a leaf changes with the light it gets.

setup.art: A bush with one leaf on a sunny outer branch and one on a shady inner branch, a hand picking each.
setup.caption: 1. Pick one leaf from a sunny branch and one from a shady branch of the same plant.

setup.art: Two leaves traced on squared paper side by side, with a child counting squares.
setup.caption: 2. Trace each leaf on squared paper. Count the squares inside.

setup.art: Two leaves held up against green crayons to match the colour.
setup.caption: 3. Match each leaf to a crayon shade. Feel the thickness.

flow.do: Ask for a guess about how the two leaves will differ. Pick the leaves.
flow.say: One leaf grew in the sun and one in the shade. How will they be different? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One leaf grew in the sun and one in the shade. How are they different? Why?

ask.q: Which leaf do you think will be bigger, and why?
good: The shade leaf, to catch more of the weak light.
The sun leaf, because it gets more food.
They will be the same.

flow.parent: Choose leaves of the same kind and about the same age. Do not correct any guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Sun Leaf and Shade Leaf. You guess before you look.

flow.do: Trace each leaf on squared paper. Count the squares inside. Match the colour to a crayon. Feel which leaf is thicker.
flow.say: Trace each leaf on the paper. Count the squares inside the line. Hold each leaf against the crayons. Which green matches?
flow.kid: Trace each leaf. Count the squares. Match the green. Feel the leaf.

ask.q: What differences did you find?
good: The shade leaf is bigger and thinner.
The shade leaf is a darker green.
The sun leaf is smaller and thicker.

flow.parent: Expected: the shade leaf is usually larger, thinner and darker, and the sun leaf is smaller, thicker and a little paler. The differences may be small. Count a square only if more than half of it is inside the line. If the leaves look the same, try a different plant. For a fairer comparison, take three leaves from the sun and three from the shade and use the average (add the three areas and divide by 3). With 2 to 4 children, each child traces and counts one pair of leaves, then the group compares results.

check.q: A shade leaf is often bigger, thinner and darker green than a sun leaf. Which is the best reason?
options: It catches as much of the weak light as possible
It wants to hide from the sun
It was given more water
It is older
check.why: In weak light, a wide, thin leaf with lots of chlorophyll catches more of the little light there is. A leaf in strong sun does not need to be as large and can be thicker to cope with the strong light.

flow.context: In this step, you measure and compare the two leaves.

flow.do: Write your claim, evidence and reasoning. Say what the plant did to adapt to the light each leaf got.
flow.say: What did you find? Why do you think the plant made leaves that are different on the same plant?
flow.kid: What did you find? Why are the leaves different on one plant?
flow.think: Each leaf grew in a different amount of light. Could a plant sense the light and change the kind of leaf they make? What does that tell you?
flow.context: In this step, you say what the two leaves show about how plants respond to light.

activities.title: From Air to Lamp Black: the carbon in a flame

materials.item: a small clay diya with a cotton wick and a spoonful of sesame or coconut oil
matches or a lighter, for the grown-up only
a steel spoon with a long handle (or a steel katori held in tongs), a thick cloth to hold it, and a steel plate to rest it on
a bowl of water and a damp cloth, in case of spills
a white sheet of paper

activities.safety: A grown-up lights the diya and holds the spoon. Keep long hair tied back and loose sleeves away from the flame. Keep the bowl of water close. The spoon gets hot, so hold it with a cloth. Never leave a lit diya alone. Use coconut oil if anyone at home is allergic to sesame. Children watch from at least one metre away and never touch the spoon until it has cooled for a few minutes. Keep the diya on a steel plate on a steady table, away from curtains and paper.

schedule.what: A grown-up lights the diya. Hold a cold spoon above the flame to catch black carbon. Talk about where it came from.

activities.record: Draw the diya, the spoon and the black patch. Write the chain: air, plant, oil, flame, soot.
activities.context: In this activity, you catch black carbon from a flame on a spoon. Then you work out that this carbon was once carbon dioxide in the air.

setup.art: A lit clay diya with a small flame on a table, with a bowl of water nearby and a grown-up lighting the wick.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up lights a diya filled with sesame oil.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a steel spoon with a cloth about 3 centimetres above the flame tip, a thin black patch forming on the spoon.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up holds a cold spoon above the tip of the flame for 5 seconds.

setup.art: A black soot patch on the spoon, and a child's finger rubbing a little on white paper to show a black smudge.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the black patch. Rub a little on white paper.

flow.do: Show the diya and the oil. Ask where the oil came from. Write down the answers.
flow.say: This oil burns and gives light. Where did the oil come from? And where did the plant get what the oil is made of?
flow.kid: This oil burns. Where did the oil come from?

ask.q: What is the oil made from? What do you think is in the flame?
good: It comes from sesame seeds or coconut.
The plant made it from sunlight and air.
The flame has heat and light.

flow.parent: Do not correct the answers. Sesame or coconut oil is pressed out of seeds or flesh that a plant made.
flow.context: This is the first step of From Air to Lamp Black. You think about where the oil came from.

flow.do: A grown-up lights the diya. Hold a cold spoon in a cloth so its underside touches the yellow flame tip for 3 to 5 seconds. Rest it on the steel plate. Try again low in the blue part and compare.
flow.say: Watch the spoon. A black patch is forming. Where could the black stuff come from?
flow.kid: A grown-up lights the diya and holds the spoon. Look for black.
flow.parent: Use a clean, cool spoon. The black soot forms on the underside of the spoon where it cools the yellow part of the flame, which has glowing bits of unburnt carbon. In the blue part near the wick there is plenty of air and the carbon burns away, so there should be much less soot. If the soot is faint, hold the spoon in the yellow tip a second longer. Take care that the spoon does not smother the flame.

check.q: The black patch on the spoon is soot, mostly carbon. Where did that carbon come from, in the end?
options: From carbon dioxide in the air, taken in by the plant
From the spoon
From the clay of the diya
From nowhere
check.why: The oil came from a plant. The plant built the oil from sugar, and the sugar from carbon dioxide in the air. The carbon in the soot is that carbon, travelling on. Matter does not come from nowhere.

flow.context: In this step, a grown-up catches soot from the flame on a spoon.

flow.do: Let the spoon cool. Rub a little soot on white paper. Draw the chain from air to soot. Talk about candles and wax.
flow.say: Let the spoon cool. Rub a little soot on the paper. This carbon was once in the air. Which plant took it in? How long ago?
flow.kid: Rub a little black on paper. This carbon was once in the air.

ask.q: A candle is made from wax that usually comes from oil under the ground. How is its soot different from the diya's soot?
good: The candle's carbon is from very old plants and plankton.
The diya's carbon is from a plant that grew recently.
Both were once carbon dioxide in the air.

flow.think: The diya's carbon was in the air last year. A candle's carbon was in the air millions of years ago. Is the flame the same?
flow.context: In this step, you work out where the carbon came from.

activities.title: Your Breath, Counted: respiration you can feel

materials.item: a clock or phone with a seconds timer
a notebook and a pencil
a helper to count

schedule.what: Count breaths at rest, after 30 jumps and after resting again. Compare.

activities.safety: Stop and sit down if you feel dizzy or breathless. Never hold your breath, and jump only on a clear, non-slippery floor.
activities.record: Make a table with your three counts of breaths in one minute. Write the biggest change and what it tells you.
activities.context: In this activity, you count how fast you breathe at rest and after exercise. This shows how respiration speeds up when your cells need more energy.

setup.art: A child sitting still and a parent counting breaths with a clock.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still for 2 minutes. Count your breaths for 1 minute.

setup.art: A child doing star jumps while a parent counts out loud.
setup.caption: 2. Do 30 jumps. Then count your breaths for 1 minute.

setup.art: A child resting again and the notebook table filling in with three numbers.
setup.caption: 3. Rest for 3 minutes. Count your breaths again. Write all three numbers.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess how many breaths they take in one minute at rest and after jumping. Write the guesses.
flow.say: How many breaths do you think you take in one minute when you sit still? And after jumping? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess your breaths in one minute, sitting and after jumping.

ask.q: Why do you think we breathe faster when we move?
good: Our body needs more air.
Our muscles use more oxygen.
We are tired.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Children at rest often take about 18 to 25 breaths a minute.
flow.context: This is the first step of Your Breath, Counted. You guess before you count.

flow.do: Count breaths for one minute sitting. Do 30 jumps. Count for one minute. Rest 3 minutes. Count again. Write all three numbers.
flow.say: Sit still for two minutes. Count each time your chest goes up. Do that for one minute. Then jump and count again.
flow.kid: Sit still and count breaths for a minute. Then jump 30 times and count again.

ask.q: What changed after the jumps? Why?
good: We breathed faster, because the muscles needed more oxygen.
More respiration is happening in the muscles.
The body needed more energy.

flow.parent: Stop at once if your child feels dizzy or unwell. Count a breath each time the chest rises. Counting together is easier than counting alone. With 2 to 4 children, work in pairs: one counts, one is counted, then swap. Count while the child reads or looks away, because people breathe differently when they watch their own breath. A resting count differs from child to child, so there is no exact right number.

check.q: Why do you breathe faster after jumping?
options: Your cells are using more oxygen and making more carbon dioxide
Your lungs have shrunk
The air has changed
You have more blood
check.why: Your muscles are doing respiration faster to release more energy. That needs more oxygen, and it makes more carbon dioxide to get rid of. Breathing faster brings the oxygen in and the carbon dioxide out.

flow.context: In this step, you count your breaths three times.

flow.do: Compare the three numbers. Work out how many more breaths you took after jumping. Talk about a plant on a hot day.
flow.say: How many more breaths did you take after jumping? A plant also respires faster when it is warm. What might happen on a very hot night?
flow.kid: How many more breaths did you take after jumping?
flow.think: Your breath out has about 100 times more carbon dioxide than the air. Where does it all go?
flow.context: In this step, you compare your counts and think about what a plant does when it is warm.

activities.title: The Pond's Day on Paper: draw a line graph of oxygen

materials.item: squared paper, a ruler and two coloured pencils
the practice data in the steps below

schedule.what: Draw two line graphs of the practice data. Find the highest and lowest points. Compare a sunny day and a cloudy day.

activities.record: Draw your graph with two lines, one for a sunny day and one for a cloudy day. Write the time of the highest and lowest oxygen on each.
activities.context: In this activity, you draw a graph of how much oxygen is in a pond over a day. The numbers are made up for practice, but they follow the pattern that real ponds show.

setup.art: A table of practice numbers: times of day down one side and oxygen readings for a sunny day and a cloudy day beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Copy the table of practice numbers.

setup.art: Squared paper with times along the bottom and oxygen up the side, dots marked for a sunny day.
setup.caption: 2. Mark a dot for each sunny day number. Join the dots.

setup.art: Two lines on one graph in two colours, the sunny day high and the cloudy day low, with a red dotted line marking the level where fish get stressed.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the cloudy day line in another colour. Mark the level where fish are stressed.

flow.do: Show the table. Ask for a guess about the shape of the line. Write the guess.
flow.say: A pond is measured every three hours for a day and a night. What shape do you think the oxygen line will make? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: What shape will the oxygen line make over a day? Why?

ask.q: When do you think the oxygen will be highest, and when lowest?
good: Highest in the afternoon, lowest at dawn.
Highest at noon.
Lowest at night.

flow.parent: These are made-up numbers for practice, in milligrams of oxygen per litre of water. The table is: Time then sunny day then cloudy day. 6 am: 3.0, 2.8. 9 am: 4.5, 3.2. 12 noon: 7.0, 4.0. 3 pm: 9.0, 4.5. 6 pm: 8.0, 4.2. 9 pm: 6.5, 3.6. 12 midnight: 5.0, 3.0. 3 am: 3.8, 2.2. 6 am the next day: 2.8, 1.5.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Pond's Day on Paper. You guess the shape before you draw.

flow.do: Draw the time along the bottom and the oxygen up the side. Mark a dot for each sunny day number. Join the dots. Do the cloudy day in another colour.
flow.say: Put the time along the bottom and the oxygen up the side. Mark each number as a dot. Join the dots with a ruler.
flow.kid: Draw the time along the bottom. Draw oxygen up the side. Mark each dot.

ask.q: When is the oxygen highest, and when is it lowest, on the sunny day? And on the cloudy day?
good: Highest at 3 pm and lowest at 6 am, on both days.
The cloudy day is lower all the way along.
On the cloudy day the lowest is much lower.

check.q: On the graph, the cloudy day line is lower than the sunny day line all day. What is the best reason?
options: Dim light means the plants and algae make less oxygen
Clouds use up oxygen from the air
Fish breathe more on cloudy days
The pond is cooler on cloudy days
check.why: Photosynthesis needs light. On a cloudy day, the pond's plants and algae make less oxygen, but everything in the pond still uses it. So the whole line sits lower.

flow.context: In this step, you draw the two lines of practice numbers.
flow.parent: With 2 to 4 children, one draws the sunny line and another the cloudy line on the same graph, then check each other's dots. A single child does both.

flow.do: Draw a dotted line at 3 for the level below which many pond fish get stressed. Find where each line goes under it. Write what you see.
flow.say: Draw a dotted line at 3. Many pond fish get stressed below about 3. Where does each line dip below it? At what time?
flow.kid: Draw a dotted line at 3. Where do the lines dip below it?

ask.q: What could a fish farmer do on a cloudy day, when the line dips below the dotted line in the night?
good: Stir or splash the water to mix in air.
Feed the fish less.
Run an aerator at night.

flow.parent: On the sunny day, the line dips to about 2.8 at the next dawn, just below 3. The cloudy day starts at 2.8, below 3, rises above 3 by 9 am, falls back to exactly 3.0 at midnight, then dips below it and reaches 1.5 at dawn. The 3 level is a rough guide. Different fish can stand different levels.
flow.think: The farmer cannot see these numbers without a meter. What signs could the fish give?
flow.context: In this step, you mark the level where fish are stressed and find the dangerous times.

projects.title: Sealed Jar Garden: a garden that recycles its own air

materials.item: a large clear glass jar with a lid, 1 to 2 litres
a handful of small pebbles or gravel
potting soil, enough for a layer about 6 centimetres deep
2 small plants or cuttings that like humid air, such as money plant or tradescantia cuttings (often free from a neighbour), or a small fern
a spoon, a spray bottle of water and a notebook
a ruler, to measure the tallest stem

projects.safety: Wash your hands after touching the soil. If mould grows, a grown-up removes it and you do not sniff it. Keep the jar out of direct sun, because a closed jar in strong sun gets hot enough to cook the plants.

schedule.what: Build the jar garden. Close the lid. Place it in bright light, out of direct sun.
Look for water drops on the glass. Draw the jar.
Look and draw. Note any new leaves, mould or wilting.
Look and draw. Compare with day 1.
Look, draw and write what the jar did without being opened for four weeks.

projects.record: Draw the jar on days 1, 7, 14 and 28. Measure the tallest stem in centimetres each time. Write how many water drops there were, whether the plants grew, and anything that went wrong.
projects.context: In this project, you seal a small garden in a jar and leave it for four weeks. You find out how plants, soil and air can recycle each other, with no new air or water.

setup.art: A jar with a layer of pebbles at the bottom, then a thick layer of soil, and a spoon adding soil.
setup.caption: 1. Put pebbles in the bottom, then soil, in a clear jar.

setup.art: Two small plants being planted in the soil with a spoon, then a light spray of water.
setup.caption: 2. Plant two small plants. Spray the soil lightly with water.

setup.art: The jar with its lid on, placed on a shelf near a window with bright light but not direct sun, with water drops on the inside of the glass.
setup.caption: 3. Close the lid. Put the jar in bright light, out of direct sun.

flow.do: Show the jar and plants. Ask what will happen to a sealed garden over four weeks. Write the guess.
flow.say: We will seal two plants in a jar for four weeks. No new air, no new water. What do you think will happen? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We seal a garden in a jar. It gets no new air or water. What will happen? Why?

ask.q: Do you think the plants will live? What will they need from outside the jar?
good: They will die because they have no new air.
They need light, which comes through the glass.
They will live because they recycle the air and water.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. The jar needs light from outside, but no air and no water.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sealed Jar Garden. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Put pebbles in the jar, then soil about 6 centimetres deep. Plant the two plants. Spray lightly with water. Close the lid.
flow.say: Put the pebbles in first. Add the soil. Plant the two plants gently. Spray the soil with water, just a little, and close the lid.
flow.kid: Add pebbles, then soil. Plant two plants. Spray lightly. Close the lid.
flow.parent: The soil should be damp, not wet. Water should not pool at the bottom. If water drips down the glass at the start, open the lid for an hour to let some out. Use plants that like moist air. Cacti and succulents will rot in a sealed jar. In the damp monsoon, mould grows easily, so spray very lightly and keep the soil a little drier. With 2 to 4 children, each builds a jar of their own, and one child can make a second jar with the lid left off and not watered, to compare with the sealed one.

check.q: Why is the jar kept in bright light but out of direct sun?
options: The plants need light, but a closed jar in strong sun gets too hot
Plants need no light in a jar
Direct sun makes the soil dry
The glass needs to stay cool for the lid
check.why: Plants need light for photosynthesis. But a sealed jar traps heat, so strong direct sun can overheat and cook the plants. Bright, indirect light is the safe middle.

flow.context: In this step, you build the jar garden and seal it.

flow.do: Place the jar in bright light. On day 2, look for water drops on the glass and draw the jar.
flow.say: Look at the inside of the glass. Do you see water drops? Where did they come from? Will they stay there?
flow.kid: Look for drops on the glass. Draw the jar.

ask.q: Where did the water drops come from, and where will they go?
good: From the soil and the leaves. They rise as vapour and turn back into drops.
They will run down and water the plants again.
It's a little rain inside the jar.

flow.context: In this step, you watch the jar make its own small water cycle.

flow.do: On day 28, compare your drawings. Write what the jar did. Do not open it before then, unless mould spreads.
flow.say: Compare the drawings. What changed? What stayed the same? Where do you think the plants got air and water from?
flow.kid: Compare the drawings. What changed? What stayed the same?

ask.q: How did the plants breathe and drink for four weeks in a sealed jar?
good: They used the air in the jar over and over.
In light, they made oxygen and used carbon dioxide. At night and in the soil, the other way round.
The water went round and round.

flow.parent: Many sealed jars last for months. A man named David Latimer is reported to have planted a bottle garden in 1960, watered it once in 1972 and then sealed it, and the plants were said to be alive decades later. If mould grows, open the lid for a day and remove it. If the plants die, that is a result too. Ask which need was missing.
flow.think: The jar had plants and soil bacteria and fungi. What do you think each does in the air cycle?
flow.context: In this step, you look back at four weeks and explain how the jar kept itself going.

challenges.title: Greenhouse Budget: spend 100 coins to grow the most tomatoes
challenges.problem: A greenhouse grower has 100 coins. Light, carbon dioxide and warmth can each be raised from level 1 to level 2 or 3, at a price. A tomato plant grows only as fast as the lowest of the three levels. Find the best way to spend the coins.
constraints: Spend no more than 100 coins in total.
Light costs 20 coins for level 2 and 50 coins for level 3. Carbon dioxide costs 30 coins for level 2 and 60 coins for level 3. Warmth costs 10 coins for level 2 and 40 coins for level 3.
Every factor starts at level 1 for free.
Growth equals the lowest of the three levels. If two plans have the same growth, the plan with the higher total of all three levels wins.
materials: a sheet of paper and a pencil
three small cards labelled Light, Carbon dioxide and Warmth
dried beans or coins as a pretend budget
a copy of the price list
general: Spend the coins evenly: raise every factor to level 2 and keep the spare coins, for growth 2.
Raise the cheapest factor first, which is warmth, then the next cheapest, and stop when you can no longer afford to raise all three.
Check that you are not spending coins on a factor that is already above the lowest.
creative: Find a free way to raise a level: for example, move the plants to the sunniest bench for free light, or open vents for free fresh air with more carbon dioxide.
Share the greenhouse with a neighbour and split the costs of carbon dioxide so that both reach level 3.
Ask which factor is the limiting one on a cloudy winter day, and change the plan for that season.
challenges.your_turn: Make your best plan on paper. Say which factor limits the growth and why spending more on another factor would be wasted. Then ask: what is the limiting factor for a plant in your own home, and what free thing could you do about it?
challenges.context: This is a paper design challenge about limiting factors. You decide how to spend a small budget so that the slowest factor does not hold the plants back.

setup.art: Three tall bars labelled light, carbon dioxide and warmth at levels 1, 2 and 3, with a flat bar across the shortest one showing the growth.
setup.caption: 1. Draw three bars, one for each factor. The shortest bar sets the growth.

setup.art: A price list beside a pile of coins, with a hand moving coins to raise one bar.
setup.caption: 2. Spend coins to raise bars. Stay under 100.

setup.art: A final plan with three bars at the same height and a tomato plant on top, with a tick.
setup.caption: 3. Check your plan. Which bar is the limit?

flow.do: Read the problem and the price list. Ask your child to say what limits a plant on a dim day. Write down the answer.
flow.say: A plant grows only as fast as the lowest of the three levels: light, carbon dioxide and warmth. If one is low, does it help to raise the other two? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A plant grows as fast as its lowest factor. Does raising the others help?

ask.q: If light is level 1, would more carbon dioxide help?
good: No, because light is still the lowest.
Not by itself.
Only if light goes up too.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Greenhouse Budget challenge. You think about limits.

flow.do: Make two or three different plans. Add up the cost and find the growth for each. Write them in a table.
flow.say: Try a few plans. Add up the cost. Find the lowest level. Which plan gives the highest growth for 100 coins?
flow.kid: Try some plans. Add the cost. Find the lowest level.

ask.q: Which plan gives the most growth, and how much does it cost?
good: Raising all three to level 2 costs 60 and gives growth 2.
Raising only light to level 3 gives growth 1, because the others are still level 1.
Level 3 for all costs 150, which is too much.

flow.parent: The most growth that 100 coins can buy is 2, because level 3 for all three costs 150. All three at level 2 costs 60. The tie-break then picks a plan with a higher total. Light 2, carbon dioxide 2 and warmth 3 costs 90 and totals 7. Light 3, carbon dioxide 2 and warmth 2 also costs 90 and totals 7. Light 3 and warmth 3 with carbon dioxide at 1 costs 90 but gives growth 1.

check.q: A grower spends 50 coins on light level 3 and leaves carbon dioxide at level 1. What is the growth?
options: 1, because carbon dioxide is still the lowest
3, because light is the highest
2, because it is the average
0, because nothing is raised
check.why: Growth is the lowest of the three levels. The 50 coins on light were wasted while carbon dioxide stayed at level 1.

flow.context: In this step, you try plans and find the growth for each.

flow.do: Choose your best plan. Write why the other plans were worse. Think of a free way to raise one factor.
flow.say: Which plan is best? Why were the others worse? Can you think of a free way to raise one factor?
flow.kid: Which plan is best? Why were the others worse?
flow.think: In a real greenhouse, a grower measures and finds out which factor limits the plants. How would you find this in a pot plant at home?
flow.context: In this step, you choose your best plan and explain it.

videos.title: Photosynthesis and Cellular Respiration - Energy Cycle of Life
videos.why: To see photosynthesis and respiration drawn side by side, and where each happens in a cell.
videos.check: Id confirmed with YouTube (title and channel match). A parent should preview it first.

videos.title: Why do fish gasp at dawn? Oxygen in a pond
videos.why: To see a graph of the oxygen in a pond over a day and a night, and what fish farmers do about it.
videos.check: Not yet found. Find one, watch it, and check that it shows the dawn low and not just the daytime high.

videos.title: T.W.Engelmann's experiment
videos.why: To see the 1882 experiment that used bacteria to show which colours of light work best.
videos.check: Id confirmed with YouTube (title and channel match). A parent should preview it first.

quiz.p: Which statement about plants and the air is the most complete?
opts: Plants respire all the time, and in good light they also photosynthesise, so overall they give out oxygen
Plants only take in carbon dioxide and only give out oxygen
Plants take in oxygen only at night and never in the day
Plants do not respire because they make their own food
quiz.why: Every living cell respires. Plants also photosynthesise when there is light, and in good light that is faster, so they give out more oxygen than they use. Making food does not stop a plant needing energy from that food.

quiz.p: A jar of blue-purple cabbage water with breath in it turns pink. A jar with the same water and breath, with leaves in the light, ends up bluer than that jar. What does this show?
opts: The leaves in the light used up carbon dioxide
The leaves gave out carbon dioxide
The light turned the water blue
The breath changed itself
quiz.why: Pink means more carbon dioxide. Bluer means less. The jar with leaves in the light lost carbon dioxide because photosynthesis used it.
quiz.context: In the Breath Colours test, you compare jars of cabbage water with and without leaves, in light and in dark.

quiz.p: When is the dissolved oxygen in a still pond usually lowest?
opts: Just before sunrise
At noon
At about three in the afternoon
Just after sunset
quiz.why: The oxygen falls through the whole night, because nothing makes any and everything uses it. It is lowest just before the sun comes up.

quiz.p: Why is warm water a problem for pond fish on a hot night?
opts: It holds less oxygen, and the living things in it use oxygen faster
It holds more oxygen, which is too much
It makes the plants stop breathing
It makes the water heavy
quiz.why: Warm water holds less dissolved gas, and the living things in warm water use oxygen faster. Both lower the oxygen at the same time.
quiz.context: In the Bubbles on the Glass test, you warm cold water and watch dissolved air come out as bubbles.

quiz.p: Where in a cell does respiration mainly happen?
opts: In the mitochondria
In the chloroplasts
In the cell wall
In the stomata
quiz.why: Mitochondria break sugar down with oxygen to release energy. Chloroplasts are where photosynthesis happens. Stomata are holes in the leaf, not parts of a cell.

quiz.p: A graph of photosynthesis rises with light, then goes flat. A grower adds carbon dioxide and the graph rises again. What was limiting the plants before?
opts: Carbon dioxide
Light
Soil colour
The age of the plant
quiz.why: The flat part means light was no longer the limit. When adding carbon dioxide made the rate rise, carbon dioxide was the limiting factor there.

quiz.p: Why do pineapples and cactuses open their stomata at night?
opts: It is cooler, so they lose less water while taking in carbon dioxide
They need moonlight to make sugar
They cannot open them in the day because they are asleep
They breathe out more oxygen at night
quiz.why: CAM plants take in carbon dioxide at night, when little water escapes, and store it. They keep the stomata shut in the hot day and use the stored carbon dioxide with sunlight.

quiz.p: Sugarcane stays green and grows fast in hot, bright weather. What helps it do so?
opts: A pump that gathers carbon dioxide, so photosynthesis stays fast even when the stomata are only a little open
More chlorophyll than any other plant
It does not need light
It does not do respiration
quiz.why: Sugarcane is a C4 plant. Its carbon dioxide pump keeps a crowd of carbon dioxide round rubisco, so it works well in heat with its stomata partly shut.

quiz.p: Coal and oil are called fossil fuels. Which is the best description of where their energy came from?
opts: Sunlight caught by plants and tiny sea creatures millions of years ago
Heat from inside the Earth only
The Moon
Electricity stored in rocks
quiz.why: The carbon in coal and oil was taken from the air by photosynthesis long ago. The stored energy is that ancient sunlight.

quiz.p: Each year, the carbon dioxide in the world's air dips in the northern spring and summer. What is the best reason?
opts: Land plants in the north are growing and taking carbon dioxide in
Fewer people breathe in summer
The air gets colder
The oceans stop taking in gas
quiz.why: Most of the land lies in the north. When the leaves open, photosynthesis pulls carbon dioxide out of the air. In autumn the leaves fall and rot, and it goes back.

quiz.p: A very green pond is always a healthy pond for fish.
quiz.why: False. A thick bloom can make the oxygen crash at night or when the bloom dies and rots. What matters is the balance of making and using oxygen.

quiz.p: In 1882, Theodor Engelmann shone a rainbow on a thread of green alga with oxygen-loving bacteria around it. Why did the bacteria gather in the red and blue parts?
opts: Those colours made the alga give out the most oxygen, and the bacteria swim towards oxygen
The bacteria like to eat red and blue light
Those colours are the warmest
Green light is poisonous to bacteria
quiz.why: The bacteria were a living instrument. They gather where there is most oxygen. The crowds in the red and blue showed that chlorophyll uses those colours best.

applications: Fish and shrimp farmers watching the oxygen in their ponds, and running aerators at night.
Greenhouse growers adding light, warmth and carbon dioxide so that no single factor limits the crop.
Breeding crops such as ragi, bajra and sugarcane that thrive in heat and dry weather.
Choosing house plants that suit a dim room, because they break even at low light.
Planting forests and protecting seaweed beds and mangroves, which take carbon out of the air.
Monitoring the Earth's plants from space, using the green colour of chlorophyll.
Understanding fuels, because the energy in coal, oil and gas was caught by photosynthesis long ago.
Designing sealed life-support systems for space stations, where plants and people pass oxygen and carbon dioxide back and forth.
Treating sewage and managing fertiliser so that ponds and lakes do not turn into dead zones.
Making artificial leaves that split water with sunlight, to make clean fuel.

spotted.text: Tiny silver bubbles on green threads or water plants in a sunny pond or tank. These are bubbles of oxygen.
spotted.art: A close-up of green pond threads in sunlight with silver bubbles clinging to them.

spotted.text: Fish coming up to the surface of a pond or tank early in the morning.
spotted.art: A garden pond at dawn with a few fish mouths at the surface.

spotted.text: A paddle wheel or a fountain at a fish farm, churning the water.
spotted.art: A paddle wheel in a shrimp pond throwing up white spray at dusk.

open_questions.q: Is photorespiration a flaw, a safety valve, or both?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists agree that it costs energy. They disagree about how much good it does, and the answer may differ from plant to plant.

open_questions.q: Could rice be given the sugarcane pump?
open_questions.why_open: A large project has been trying since 2008. The pump needs many changes in leaf shape and chemistry, and no one has finished it yet.

open_questions.q: How much of the carbon dioxide we put into the air will land plants and the sea keep taking in?
open_questions.why_open: Plants and the sea have taken up a large share so far. Scientists do not agree on how long that will last as the world warms.

open_questions.q: How do plants and algae decide when to open and close their stomata over the day?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know parts of the signals, such as light, water and carbon dioxide. They are still working out how the leaf combines them.

open_questions.q: Could photosynthesis work on a planet around a red star, where the light is redder and weaker?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think plants there might look dark or even black. Nobody has yet seen a plant on another planet to check.

open_questions.q: How did the first living things that made oxygen survive their own waste?
open_questions.why_open: Oxygen is harmful to many cells that did not evolve with it. Scientists have clues from ancient rocks, but the story is far from complete.
